docs.text: Job Settings Each tab saves separately. The floating Save button saves only the tab you're on. A dot on a tab means it still has unsaved changes — save each dotted tab before you leave. I changed a setting, switched tabs, and my change was gone. Why? Each tab saves on its own. When you switch tabs with unsaved changes, you're asked whether to discard them — choosing to move on drops them. Press Save first (or answer Stay at the prompt) to keep your changes. Where's the Save button? It only appears when the tab you're on has unsaved changes — a floating Save button at the bottom-right. It saves that one tab, so if several tabs have dots, save each of them. The "Allow ... Registration" toggle is greyed out. How do I turn registration on or off? Those switches — player, team, and staff/coach registration, plus public schedule and roster access — are managed in Quick Links . They show here read-only so you can see the current state without two screens disagreeing. Change them in Quick Links and they update here. What does the padlock icon mean? A padlock marks a SuperUser-only field. Directors can see it but can't change it — things like processing fees, sport / customer / billing type, recurring billing, and store settings. Why can't I turn on eCheck? eCheck rides on check payments, so Check must be an allowed method first — set Allowed Methods to CC or Check or Check Only , then the Enable eCheck box unlocks. Note the processing and eCheck fees themselves are SuperUser-only. Where did the "full payment required" setting go? It's no longer a single job-wide switch. Full-payment phase is now set per league, age group, or team on the fee cards (the most specific scope wins), so different divisions can differ. Existing job-level values are still honored as the fallback. On the Adult tab, what does "Apply coach form change" do? Picking a different coach form and applying it rebuilds the form from that template — it's a structural swap, not a field tweak. To edit individual fields on the existing form, use Profile Editor → Adult instead. “Require USA Lacrosse #” is only available on forms that support it. How do invitation tokens work? When Require Invitation Token is on (Players or Teams tab), registrants need a valid invite link to start. Generate those links in batch emails with !INVITE_LINK for players and !CLUBREP_INVITE_LINK for club reps. With the token off, registration is open to anyone. What size should banner images be? Upload the banner background at 1920 × 422 (50:11) so it fits without cropping. The overlay image is resized to max 800px wide and the header logo to max 400px wide. If “Use custom banner images” is off, a default TSIC banner shows instead. How do I add several dropdown options at once? On the Dropdowns tab, type multiple values separated by semicolons in the add box and they're added in bulk. These values feed the dropdowns on the player and team registration forms. Can I change the order of dropdown options? Yes — registrants see the options in the order shown on the Dropdowns tab. Drag a chip to a new position, or use its ‹ › arrows to nudge it one spot at a time. Changes take effect when you save. What are player and team donations? Enabling them (Payment tab) adds an optional donation field to the payment page. Any amount entered is charged in full, plus processing , together with the registrant's payment. Tip: setting up a new event? Walk the tabs left to right — General, Branding, Payment, then the registration tabs — saving as you go. The dots tell you which tabs you've touched but not yet saved.

docs.text: LADT editor — FAQ What does "LADT" stand for? L eagues, A ge Groups, D ivisions, T eams — the four levels of the event tree, in the order they nest. A league contains age groups, an age group contains divisions, and a division contains teams. How do I add an age group, division, or team? Hover the parent branch and click its button — a blank row appears right where the new item will live. Type a name and press Enter to create it, or Esc to back out. You add age groups from a league, divisions from an age group, and teams from a division. Why can't I delete this age group or division? An age group or division can be removed only when it has no teams beneath it — the button is hidden while any remain, so you don't strand teams. Move or remove the teams first. The Unassigned division is permanent and can never be deleted. What happens when I remove a team? It depends on whether the team has any history. If it has no players, payments, or schedule records , it's deleted permanently. If it does, it isn't erased — it's moved to the Dropped Teams bucket and deactivated, so its registrations and payment trail stay intact. Why is a fee shown faded, or labeled "inherited"? Fees cascade down the tree — Job → League → Age Group → Team — and the most specific level that actually sets a value wins. A faded pill means this row didn't set that fee itself; it's inherited from a level above. Hover the to see whether it was set here or inherited, and from which level. What do "Single", "Deposit", and "PIF" mean in the Payment Phase column? Single Deposit PIF Single — one charge, because the fee has only a deposit or only a balance. Deposit — a deposit now with the balance due later. PIF (paid in full) — the whole amount is required up front. The phase only matters when a fee carries both a deposit and a balance to split; otherwise it always reads Single. How do I control whether registrants pay a deposit first or the full amount? With the Payment Phase choice on a fee card, at any level. Below league it has three options: Use league / age group setting follows the level above, Deposit first means deposit now and balance later — regardless of any higher-level setting — and Full payment now collects everything at registration. At league level there's nothing above to follow, so it's simply Deposit first or Full payment now. Like fee amounts, the most specific level that sets a phase wins; when no level sets one, registrants pay the deposit first. Why don't I see the Payment Phase options on a fee card? The phase can only matter where a deposit exists to split from the balance. If no deposit is configured anywhere the card's setting reaches, the radios are replaced by a one-line Single payment note telling you exactly what gets charged. Enter a deposit — here or at a level the card governs — and the full control comes back. My league says one thing, but an age group or team charges differently. How do I see that? The cards disclose the cascade in both directions. When a card follows a higher level, it says so: "Currently: Full payment now — set at league level." And when levels below set their own values, the card names them: "2 age groups set their own phase: U12 (Full payment), U14 (Deposit first)" — with matching lines under the amounts and the Early Bird / Late Fee section. A league card even looks past its age groups: a team two levels down with its own setting shows up as "Plus 1 team further down sets its own phase." And when nothing below goes its own way, the card says that too: "No age group or team in this league sets its own phase, amounts, or Early Bird / Late Fee — this card governs them all." (Dropped Teams and WAITLIST buckets are holding areas, not choices someone made — they never count as overrides.) The grid shows the same story per row: faded pills are inherited, and the tooltip names the level that set each value. What happens to people who already registered when I change a fee or the phase? Saving asks you, right in the save bar. For an amount or discount change : Update all reprices existing unpaid registrations too (the usual intent), while Future only leaves them at the old price. A phase change always converts existing registrations so everyone is on the same payment plan, with a count of how many are affected. The flip applies to the card you're on — to change the phase for the whole league, set it on the league card and it flows down to every age group that doesn't set its own. Money already collected is never changed — repricing only adjusts what's still owed. What does "Theme Division Names" do? It's a bulk way to name divisions the same across every age group. Open it from the menu, enter a list of names (classic Pool A, Pool B or any theme), and each age group's divisions are renamed to match — creating new divisions where an age group has fewer than your list. It shows a full preview first, and a division that already has teams is locked so it won't be renamed away. What are the "Dropped Teams" and "WAITLIST" buckets? They're holding areas, not real age groups — so they sit at the bottom of the tree and look different. Dropped Teams collects teams removed from active play (with their history preserved), and WAITLIST holds teams awaiting a spot. You won't add or edit divisions inside them the way you would a normal age group. Is there a fast way to move between teams while editing? Yes. With the detail panel open, use the ▲ / ▼ arrow keys or the dropdown in the panel header to step through siblings without closing it. If you have unsaved edits, it asks before moving on so nothing is lost. Why does the Club column sometimes not appear? The Club column shows only when the event actually has teams from more than one club. For a single-club event it's hidden to keep the grid clean. How do I recolor an age group? Click the color dot to the left of the age group's name in the tree and pick a swatch (or "none"). The color applies immediately and flows down to that age group's divisions, so related items read together in the tree and in scheduling. Tip: setting a fee once at the league or age group level lets every team below inherit it — you only drop to team-level fees for the exceptions.

docs.text: The LADT editor LADT is the structural backbone of an event — its L eagues, A ge Groups, D ivisions, and T eams. This screen is where you build and maintain that hierarchy: add and rename branches, set fees, recolor age groups, and edit a single team without losing your place. The four levels Every event is a tree four levels deep. Each level is the parent of the one below it: League Age Group Division Team How it works Pick any item in the tree on the left. The grid on the right lists everything at that level — the item's siblings — with their counts and fees. Click a row (or a tree item) to open its detail panel , where you edit its fields. The header shows event-wide totals — teams and players — plus how many active teams are waitlisted, scheduled, or neither. Use Expand / Collapse to open or close the whole tree, and Refresh to reload it. Building the structure Hover a branch and click the to add a child — an age group under a league, a division under an age group, a team under a division. A new row appears inline; type a name and press Enter to keep it or Esc to cancel. From the grid you can also Clone a team or a whole age group — a fast way to stand up a second bracket or a returning division without rebuilding it by hand. Fees at a glance For leagues, age groups, and teams the grid shows the resolved Deposit / Balance , Early Bird Discount , Late Fee , and Payment Phase . Fees cascade down the tree — Job → League → Age Group → Team — and the most specific level that sets a value wins. A pill shown faded is inherited from a level above; hover its to see exactly where it came from. Single Deposit PIF Payment Phase tells you how a registrant pays: Single — one charge (the fee has only a deposit or only a balance); Deposit — pay a deposit now, the balance later; PIF — the full amount is required up front. The phase only splits when a fee carries both a deposit and a balance. Editing fees in the detail panel Open a league, age group, or team and you'll find a fee card per role — Player and Club Rep / Team . Leaving Deposit or Balance Due blank means "inherit" — the field's placeholder shows the value coming from the level above, and typing an amount overrides it from this level down. A role with no fees anywhere in the event collapses to an Add … Fees link so unused cards stay out of the way. The Payment Phase choice cascades the same way. Below league level it offers three options: Use league / age group setting (follow the level above), Deposit first (deposit now, balance later — regardless of any higher-level setting), and Full payment now . At league level — the top — there's nothing above to follow, so the choice is simply Deposit first or Full payment now. When no level sets anything, registrants pay the deposit first. The phase radios appear only where they can matter — that is, where a deposit exists somewhere the setting reaches. With no deposit configured anywhere, the card shows a one-line Single payment note instead; set a deposit to enable two-phase payment. Seeing the cascade in both directions Every fee card tells you where its values come from and where they've been overridden: From above — when a card follows the level above, it states the outcome plainly: "Currently: Full payment now — set at league level." From below — when more specific levels go their own way, the card names them: "2 age groups set their own phase: U12 (Full payment), U14 (Deposit first)." The same lines appear for amounts and for Early Bird / Late Fee, so a league card never reads as governing everything when it doesn't. A league card checks its teams too — one with its own setting two levels down appears as "Plus 1 team further down…" Dropped Teams and WAITLIST buckets never count as overrides; they're holding areas, not choices someone made. All clear — and when nothing below sets its own value, the card says that too: "No age group or team in this league sets its own phase, amounts, or Early Bird / Late Fee — this card governs them all." Change the card with confidence; what you set here is what everyone gets. Early Bird Discounts & Late Fees Each fee card can carry one Early Bird Discount and one Late Fee , and each must have both a start and an end date — the window is what gives it meaning. The card warns you if the two windows overlap (a registrant in the overlap would receive both). Changing fees when people have already registered Saving a change that affects existing registrations asks you what to do, right in the save bar. An amount or discount change offers Update all (reprice existing unpaid registrations too — the usual intent) or Future only . A phase flip always converts existing registrations so everyone is on the same plan, with a count of who's affected. A flip applies to the card you're on; to change the phase league-wide, set it on the league card — it flows to every age group that doesn't set its own. Colors & division themes Click the color dot beside an age group to give it a color — its divisions pick up the same tint, so the tree (and later, schedules) reads at a glance. The gear menu's Theme Division Names names divisions across every age group at once: type a set of names ( Pool A, Pool B… or a fun theme) and each age group's divisions are renamed to match, with new ones created where an age group is short. It previews every change before you apply it. Removing things Leagues can't be deleted here. Age groups and divisions can be deleted only when no teams sit beneath them; the is hidden otherwise. The Unassigned division is permanent. Removing a team is safe: if it has no players, payments, or schedule history it's deleted outright; otherwise it's moved to Dropped Teams and deactivated so its records survive. Good to know Dropped Teams and WAITLIST buckets always sort to the bottom of the tree and are styled apart — they're holding areas, not editable age groups. With the detail panel open, step through siblings with the ▲ / ▼ keys or the dropdown in its header — no need to close and reopen. Unsaved edits prompt before you leave. The Club column appears only when the event has teams from more than one club.

docs.text: Pro tips Advanced features on this screen, organized by where you find them. Click any title to expand it. LADT Tree Add anywhere, inline No add-forms. Hover a node and click its — a blank row opens right in the tree at that spot. Type the name, press Enter, and the new league, age group, division, or team exists, already selected: 2027 A Escape cancels. The tree expands to show the new node and opens its detail panel. Age group colors Click the color dot next to an age group to open a swatch picker: … The color follows the age group everywhere it appears — its divisions inherit the dot in the tree, and the scheduling views use the same palette, so "2027 is red" stays true from here to the master schedule. Theme Division Names The menu's Theme Division Names renames divisions across the whole event to a consistent scheme — and shows you every proposed change before anything happens: A Red B White Nothing applies until you approve the full preview — it's a dry run you can walk away from. Resize the panels to fit your work Both side panels — the tree on the left and the detail fly-in on the right — have a drag handle on their inner edge: Tree Grid Detail fly-in Widen the tree for long club-team names, or the fly-in for fee work — each width is remembered per browser, so the layout greets you the way you left it. Sibling grid Breadcrumb navigation The badges above the grid are the selected row's ancestry — and every one is clickable, jumping the grid to that level: Aim Players 2025-2026 2027 A Each row's menu completes the moves: jump up to the parent, or drill down into a row's children — so you can tour the whole hierarchy without touching the tree. New fee features: Early Bird & Late Fee, per role Fees are no longer one number. Every level can carry, separately for Players and Club Reps : Fees — the base charge, shown as deposit–balance when two-phase Early Bird — a discount that applies before the deadline you set Late Fee — a surcharge that applies after its deadline Payment Phase — pay-in-full vs deposit-first Fees Player: $150–$350 Club Rep: $600 Early Bird Player: −$25 Late Fee Player: +$50 Payment Phase Player: Deposit Club Rep: PIF All four appear as their own columns at every level of the grid, so a whole league's money posture is readable in one screen. Set them in the detail fly-in; read them here. Where fees and phases come from A team's real price can be set on the team, its division, its age group, or the league — the pills tell you which , at a glance: Solid pill — the value is set at this level and operates here. Dimmed pill — inherited from a level above; this row adds nothing. ↓3 same — three overrides exist below, all agreeing with this value. ↓2 varies — overrides below disagree — the row's number isn't the whole story. This is the pill to chase. varies — no single value covers what's underneath; drill down to see the spread. Hover any pill's and the tooltip names the exact source level and what happens below. A pill only ever claims a value that actually operates on someone — placeholder zeros don't masquerade as pricing. Tip: the detail fly-in tells the same story — open any node and its fee cards show the resolved values with the same source context, right where you'd edit them. Clone from the row menu The menu on team and age-group rows offers cloning: Clone team duplicates the team — club-rep link handled for you Clone age group copies the whole structure underneath in one step Cloning an age group is the fast way to stand up a new season bracket that mirrors an existing one — structure first, then adjust. Column headers explain themselves The columns that carry policy — the money columns, payment phase, third-party access — have an in their header. Hover it and the column explains exactly what it controls: Early Bird Late Fee Payment Phase No manual required for a column you've never used — the header is the manual. Detail fly-in Repricing: all registrations, or future only Change a fee that touches people who already registered, and the save bar asks the question that matters before anything commits: This change affects existing registrations. Update all Future only Keep editing Update all — retroactive: everyone already registered is repriced to the new amount. This is the default, because a fee correction usually should reach the people already in. Future only — existing registrations keep the price they signed up under; only new registrations get the new amount. Keep editing — backs out; nothing saves. Flipping a payment phase is stricter: the flip reaches existing registrations only when you click Convert — Cancel reverts the toggle entirely. Unsaved changes can't slip away Edited a detail panel and clicked somewhere else? The fly-in won't silently discard your work — it stops and asks: Discard unsaved changes? This panel has changes you haven't saved. Leaving now will discard them. Keep editing Discard changes So you can navigate the tree and grid freely mid-edit — the guard catches you before anything is lost, everywhere in this editor.

My password is right but it still says invalid. The error covers both fields, so a wrong username looks identical to a wrong password. Check the username spelling, Caps Lock , and stray spaces. Still stuck? Use "Forgot your password?" to rule the password out. Do I sign in with my email or a username? The top field is your username . For some accounts that's an email address; for others it's a name you chose. Use whatever you set when the account was created. The error message vanished while I was reading it. docs.text: Manual ARB Sweep — FAQ A dry run proves what the sweep would do . It cannot prove the emails are well written. Wrong wording renders perfectly. Read the message bodies as a parent would, not just the counts. Why does my button say “Dry run”? Where is the switch to make it send? There isn't one, by design. The mode follows the server: production sends, every other server renders. A switch would be one more thing that can be left in the wrong position, and the wrong position on production is severe — a whole morning's payments not booked, while the run still reports success. Making it impossible to ask for is safer than making it easy to get right. Does a dry run send anything at all? One message, to support only: the digest, subject-prefixed [DRY RUN] . No family is ever written to — that is the line a dry run keeps, and it is about who receives mail, not about whether any mail leaves the box. The digest is sent rather than only shown because sending is the only way to test the delivery path: the mail service, the transport hop, and how a mail client renders the HTML. That transport is where the digest was being corrupted — rows arriving with tags broken mid-word — and no on-screen preview could have caught it. Everything meant for families is on screen instead: expand any row under “Family emails” to read the exact message that would have gone out. Then is a dry run looking at fake data? No. It reads the real production Authorize.Net batches — the same transactions the 4 AM pass would see — and resolves each one against real registrations, real families and real balances. It is a read-only look at live data. Only the writing and the sending are withheld. This matters because the alternative was worse than useless: before, an off-production run quietly queried the Authorize.Net test account, found nothing, and reported a clean morning — indistinguishable from a real clean morning, and from a broken sweep. What are the [DRY RUN] rows in the Email Log? A dry run still records what it would have sent, so you can review it in the Email Log the same way you review any other batch. Those rows are prefixed [DRY RUN] precisely so nobody — you, a director, or a parent looking at their own sent-mail list — ever mistakes a rendered message for one that actually went out. They only exist on non-production servers, and that database is a restored copy, so they disappear at the next refresh from production. I ran it, but the Email Log shows nothing. Where did the entries go? They went to the jobs they belong to. This screen runs across every job , but the Email Log screen shows one job at a time — whichever you are currently in. So a run that wrote entries for four other jobs looks empty from here. That is what the Email log entries table under the results is for: it lists every job that received one, with the message type and the counts. Use it to know which jobs to switch into. Why is there one log entry per job instead of one per family? Same as any batch email sent from Search Registrations: one entry per job, per message type, listing every recipient with a count. A morning where one job had both a live-plan failure and a dead-plan failure produces two entries for that job, because those are two different messages. Looking up a single family still works exactly as before — their address is matched inside the recipient list, so the family's record and their own sent-mail view both find it. The log entry shows !PLAYER and !OWEDNOW instead of real names. Is that a bug? No. A batch entry stores the message template , not any one family's copy — the same as every other batch email in the system. Each family's actual email is personalised with their player, their username and their balance, so no single stored copy could represent the batch, and picking one family's to stand in for everyone else's would be misleading. To read the finished, personalised messages, use the dry run on this screen — it shows every one of them in full. Which steps does a dry run skip? Exactly three, and only because they move money: the eCheck settlement stamp, the return reversal, and the stale-draft watchdog, which can settle or reverse a draft that went silent. Their digest sections say “not run on a dry run” rather than showing a zero or a green tick, because a zero next to “eCheck Returns” reads as “nothing bounced last night” — on a dry run that would be a claim nobody checked. Orphan detection and the eCheck integrity net do run. Both are report-only — a query and a list — so there was never a reason to withhold them, and their counts on a dry run are as real as on the 4 AM pass. ARB Activity is different — it is fully populated on a dry run, all of it, because a dry run resolves every recurring draft exactly as the 4 AM pass does. It briefly resolved only the failures to save time; that made the run useless as a rehearsal, since the settled drafts are the ones that book money. One of the emails says Reply-To “none”. What does that mean? No director with an email address could be found for that job, so a family replying to the notice would reach TSIC support instead of their own club. Worth fixing at the source — give that job an active director with a valid address — because the family is replying about their own money. If I run the sweep twice, do families get emailed twice? No. A transaction that has already been imported is recognised and skipped before it ever reaches the notification step, so a second run the same morning writes to nobody. The dry run inherits the same behaviour. A family whose card fails again on the next installment is a new failed transaction, and does get a new notice. That is intended — it is a new failure. Some families are listed as NOT emailed. Why weren't they just sent something? Because the email would not have worked. The four reasons: no sendable address on the account; no family username, so the sign-in instructions would be blank; the registrant has opted out of email; or the send itself failed. A notice telling someone to sign in as nothing produces a support call, not a payment. They are named on screen and in the digest so a person can pick them up by phone. That list is the real output of the run. Why can't I trigger the expiring-card pass on production? It writes to thousands of families across every job with a live subscription, and it is scheduled on the 2nd and the 15th exactly so that sending it is not a decision anyone makes. A button on production would add only one capability: sending it a second time, or on the wrong day, with no way to take it back. Use the dry run here to see who is in scope and what they would receive. The pass itself stays on its timer. How many days prior should I use? 1 unless you have a reason. That matches what runs nightly. Widen it to review a window you think was missed, or after an outage. Nothing is double-counted — already-processed transactions are skipped — so a bigger number costs time, not accuracy. It says “Sweep already running”. Only one pass may run at a time, and a second request is refused rather than queued — two passes at once could each decide the same transaction was unbooked and book it twice. Wait for the first to finish and run again. The banner says the mode could not be determined. The server did not answer when asked which mode it runs in. Do not click until you know — on production that button sends real mail to real families. Reload the page; if it persists, the API is likely down or unreachable, which is worth resolving before running a reconciliation pass anyway.

docs.text: Manual ARB Sweep Every morning at 4 AM a background pass reads Authorize.Net's settled batches and reconciles them against our books. This screen runs that same pass on demand. It is the only manual entry point to it, and it is SuperUser‑only. What this button does depends entirely on which server you are on. On production it books money and emails families. Anywhere else it only looks and reports. You do not choose — the server does, and the banner at the top of the page tells you which one you are looking at before you click. The seven things the sweep does Imports recurring (ARB) charges — each installment that drafted overnight is booked against the registration, and the subscription's status is re-synced from Authorize.Net. Stamps eCheck settlements — status only. eCheck money books when it is submitted; this records that the draft actually entered the banking network. Reverses eCheck returns — an NSF or closed account comes back days later, and the booked payment is backed out. Flags orphan charges — money that settled at Authorize.Net with no matching accounting row here. Reported for a human, never auto-booked. Expect zero. Runs the stale-draft watchdog — a draft that went silent instead of settling or returning. This is the only detector for one that died before it ever reached the bank. Reports untracked eCheck payments — review only. Expect zero. Emails the family behind every recurring draft that failed. This is the newest step and the reason the dry run exists. The failed-draft notice When a family's installment is declined, Authorize.Net keeps retrying, so the subscription stays active — which meant these failures never showed up in the old warning lists. Nobody was told. Now the family gets an email the same morning, telling them which payment failed, what is owed, and the exact steps to fix it. Which message they get depends on whether their plan is still alive: Plan still alive “Update Your Payment Information” — update the card and clear the balance in one step, which also restarts their future automatic payments. Plan already ended “Pay Balance Due” — there is no live plan left to repair, so they are sent straight to paying what they owe. Some families cannot be written to — no address on file, no username to give them, or they have opted out of email. Those are never guessed at: they are listed by name, on screen and in the digest, for someone to phone. Live vs. dry run The mode follows the server and cannot be switched. That is deliberate: a checkbox's only real ability is to be in the wrong state, and the wrong state here is a morning of payments silently not booked. Dry run — every server except production Reads the real production Authorize.Net batches and works out exactly what the 4 AM pass would do — then does none of it. Nothing is booked, nothing is settled, no email is sent. Instead the digest and every would-be family email are shown on screen for you to read. Live — production only The real pass. Books charges, settles and reverses eChecks, emails families, mails the digest to support. There is no undo. The banner is red and the button says Run sweep (LIVE) . Reading a dry-run result Counts Who was missed The emails The digest Checked — transactions in the batches for the window you asked for. ARB Resolved — recurring transactions worked out in full. On a live run this label reads ARB Imported , because there it also books them. Failed Drafts / Would Email / NOT Emailed — the three that matter. Found minus emailed is the number of families a person still has to contact by hand. eCheck Settled, eCheck Returns, Orphans — hidden on a dry run. Those steps do not run at all, so showing zeros would only invite you to read them as good news. Below the counts: the by-name list of families nobody could reach, then every rendered email — click one to expand it and see the recipients, the Reply-To director and the full message as the family would receive it — and finally the digest as support would get it. The expiring-card pass A second, separate job runs unattended on the 2nd and the 15th of each month. It asks Authorize.Net which cards expire this month across every job holding a live subscription, and writes to those families before the payment fails. It has its own summary to support. On a dry-run server you get a button for it. On production you do not, and that is on purpose: it mails thousands of people, it is scheduled precisely so nobody has to decide to send it, and a manual trigger would only be a way to send it twice or on the wrong day. Not the 1st — that morning belongs to the month-end close alone. Days prior How far back to ask Authorize.Net for settled batches. 1 day matches the nightly cadence and is the right answer almost always. Raise it to catch up after an outage, or to look at a window you think was missed. Already-processed transactions are recognised and skipped, so a wider window costs time, not correctness. Only one sweep runs at a time. If a pass is already in flight the request is refused rather than queued, and you will see “Sweep already running”. Wait and try again.

docs.text: Master Schedule This screen shows the schedule — it doesn't edit it. Build games on the hub's Schedule segment and move individual games in the Rescheduler; use this view to review and export the result. How do I switch between days? Use the day tabs across the top of the grid. Each tab shows one day; fields are the columns and times run down the left, so a cell is the game at that field and time. Can I export just one day instead of the whole event? Yes. Export Day downloads only the day you're currently viewing; Export Full downloads every day in a single Excel workbook. Both come out as .xlsx files. The grid is huge and hard to navigate. Is there a faster way? Press M to open the minimap — a scaled-down map of the whole grid. Click anywhere on it to jump there, and press Esc to close it. A game is in the wrong slot. How do I fix it from here? You don't fix it here — this is a read view. To move a single game use the Rescheduler ; to rebuild or delete games switch to the Schedule segment. Then come back to Master to confirm and re-export. A day is missing or the grid is blank. Why? Master only shows games that have been built and dated. A blank grid or absent day usually means those games haven't been generated yet — check the Schedule segment, or open the Scheduling Checklist , which names exactly what's still missing. I opened this from the checklist and landed in the Schedule hub. Is that right? Yes. Master is one of the hub's four segments, so the checklist's Master Schedule tool opens the hub with Master already selected. The grid, the minimap, and both exports are all exactly the same — you just get the segment control and the build surface a click away. Tip: run QA before you export a schedule for distribution. The exported workbook is exactly what people will play from, so it's worth confirming there are no conflicts first.

headings: Mobile Scorers
What can a scorer account actually do?
How do I give someone scoring access?
How do I revoke access without deleting the account?
Where do the scores they enter show up?
I don't see this feature. Why?
docs.text: Mobile Scorers These accounts are logins for the mobile scoring app. Hand one to each person entering scores; results they post flow straight into your schedule. What can a scorer account actually do? Enter game scores from the mobile app — and that's it. A scorer login doesn't open the admin site or any other tools, so it's safe to hand out to volunteers and field marshals. How do I give someone scoring access? Add a scorer to create a login, then share those credentials with the person who'll enter scores. They sign into the mobile scoring app with it. Create separate accounts where you can, so it's clear who posted what. How do I revoke access without deleting the account? Switch the account to inactive . It keeps the record but stops the login from working — handy at the end of an event, or if you want to pause someone temporarily. Delete only when you're sure you won't reuse it. Where do the scores they enter show up? In the same place as scores you'd type yourself — the schedule. Standings and brackets update from them, so a scorer keeping up on their phone keeps the whole event's results live. I don't see this feature. Why? Mobile scoring is a per-event capability. If it's not turned on for this job, the scorer tools won't appear. A SuperUser can confirm whether the mobile feature is enabled for the event. Tip: set up your scorer accounts a day or two before the event and test one login in the app. Sorting out credentials on Saturday morning is the last thing you want while games are starting.

docs.text: Mobile Scorers Manage the accounts that let people enter live game scores from the mobile scoring app . Each scorer here is a login you hand to a field marshal, volunteer, or official so they can post results in real time — which is what keeps standings and brackets current during the event. Managing accounts Add a scorer to create a login (a username and credential) to give to whoever's entering scores. Edit an account to update its details, and switch it Active on or off to grant or revoke access without deleting it. Delete an account you no longer need. How it fits the event Scores entered through the mobile app flow straight into the schedule — the same results you'd type on the View Schedule screen. Setting up scorers ahead of time means your on-site crew can keep the scoreboard live without an admin at a laptop. Common mistakes Not deactivating after the event. Flip accounts to inactive (or delete them) once the tournament's over so old logins can't post scores later. Sharing one account for everyone. Their access is limited to scoring; anything more is done from the admin site.

docs.title: Manage Pairings
headings: Manage Pairings
Why don't I see team names in the pairings?
What does "by pool size" mean?
How many games will each team play?
The scheduler won't build a division. Could pairings be the cause?
How do I change which teams meet?
docs.text: Manage Pairings Pairings are set by pool size and by rank — not per team. One table per team-count covers every division of that size; the actual teams come from each division's ranking. Why don't I see team names in the pairings? Because a pairing table is defined by rank — "Rank 1 vs Rank 4" — so it can apply to every division of that pool size at once. Each division's own rankings fill in the real teams when the schedule builds. What does "by pool size" mean? A table is keyed to the number of teams in a pool. Your 4-team divisions all share the 4-team table, your 5-team divisions share the 5-team table, and so on. That's why you define pairings once per distinct pool size rather than once per division. How many games will each team play? That's the number of rounds in the table — each round is one game per team. Set it to what your event guarantees for pool play, then use Add Block if you need to extend the pattern. The scheduler won't build a division. Could pairings be the cause? Rarely — a missing table is generated automatically at build time, and the hub's Setup incomplete panel offers to generate them on the spot. If a division still won't build, the cause is usually upstream: unpooled teams, no play dates, or no timeslots. The Scheduling Checklist names which one. How do I change which teams meet? Adjust the teams' ranks (Edit Team). Since matchups are rank-based, re-ranking a team changes which rounds it lands in — that's the lever for balancing who plays whom, rather than editing individual games. Tip: settle pool sizes (via Pool Assignment) before finalizing pairings. Change a division's team count later and it needs a different table — getting pools stable first saves reworking pairings.

docs.text: Manage Pairings Pairings define who plays whom — the round-by-round matchup pattern the scheduler uses to generate games. They're set up by pool size , not per team: one table for 4-team pools, one for 5-team pools, and so on. Every division of that size uses the same table. Reached from step 2 of the Scheduling Checklist . The arrow beside the title takes you back. Pairings are by rank, not by team. A row like "Rank 1 vs Rank 4" applies to every division of that pool size — the actual teams are filled in from each division's ranking. How a pairing table reads Pick a division to view the pairing table that applies to its pool size. Each round lists its matchups as Division Rank vs Division Rank — the #1 team plays the #4 team, etc. Set the number of rounds to control how many games each team plays in pool play. Add Block extends the pattern; Championship rows define playoff matchups sized for the pool. Why pool size matters Because a table is keyed to team count, defining pairings for each distinct pool size in your event is what lets the scheduler build round-robin games. The Scheduling Checklist reports which pool sizes still have no table — but as an informational step, not a blocker. You don't have to visit this screen. Any pool size without a table is generated automatically when the schedule builds, and the hub's setup-check panel can generate them on demand. Come here when you want to review or customize the pattern — a specific matchup order, extra rounds, a championship block — not because something is missing. Editing teams You can adjust a team's rank or name from here ( Edit Team ). Since pairings are rank-based, a team's rank is what decides which matchups it lands in — so ranking is how you shape the strength of each round. Common mistakes Missing a pool size. If a division's size has no pairing table, the scheduler can't build its games. Cover every distinct pool size. Expecting to pick teams directly. You set the rank pattern; teams flow in from each division's rankings. Too few rounds. The round count is the number of pool-play games per team — set it to what your event promises.

docs.text: Registration Protection — questions What is Registration Protection / Regsaver? It's insurance on your registration fees, provided by Vertical Insure. If a player can't participate for a covered reason, you can file a claim to recover the fees. This page is where you add it to players who aren't covered yet. How much does it cost? There's no fixed price — Vertical Insure quotes each player based on their registration. The accepted quotes add up to the Premium total shown before you pay, so you always see the amount first. Can I cover just one of my players? Yes. Accept protection for the players you want and decline the rest. You need at least one accepted to continue — if you decline everyone, the page reminds you to choose at least one or return to the event. It says every player is already covered. Then there's nothing to buy — each registered player on your account already has protection or isn't eligible for this event. You can return to the event home. Why am I asked to sign in? Protection is tied to the players on your family account , so you sign in with your family credentials to see them. If you're already signed in for this event, you skip straight to the offer. A "not a family account" message means those credentials aren't a family login. How do I know it worked? You'll see a "Protection purchased" confirmation, and Vertical Insure emails your policy details shortly after. If a purchase fails, the page shows the reason so you can try again.

How is this different from the Roster Swapper?

docs.text: Team Pool Assignment Divisions are the pools your teams play in. Sort teams into divisions here, and scheduling builds round-robin games within each one. The checklist says I have unpooled teams. Where are they? In a division called Unassigned inside the age group the checklist named. Teams land there automatically when nothing has placed them yet. Pick Unassigned in one panel and the real pool in the other, and move them across. This matters more than it looks: the schedule builder has no pairing pattern for Unassigned , so it skips those teams without complaining. That's exactly why step 1 of the checklist locks the build until the division is empty. How is this different from the Roster Swapper? Same two-panel layout, different thing being moved. The Roster Swapper moves players between teams; this screen moves whole teams between divisions (pools). Here you're shaping the competition structure, not a team's roster. What is a "symmetrical swap" and why is it asking for one? The division you're moving a team into is already full. To keep both pools within size, the preview asks you to send a team back the other way — a one-for-one swap instead of a plain transfer. Pick the team to return, and confirm. What does the Transfer Preview show me? Exactly what the move will do before it happens: which teams change divisions, whether a swap is required, and any Club Rep Impact . Nothing changes until you confirm from the preview, so it's a safe place to check your work. How do I keep the pools balanced? Sort by the Rank / rating columns and spread the stronger teams across divisions rather than stacking them together. On lacrosse events those columns come from national ranking data, so you can balance by real strength before you move anyone. I don't see the division I want in the picker. Divisions are grouped by age group in the dropdown — scroll to the right age group to find it. If a division doesn't exist yet, create it in the L-A-D-T Editor first, then come back to populate it. Can I reassign pools after the schedule is built? You can move teams, but it's disruptive — divisions drive the round-robin games and the bracket seeds, so changing them after scheduling means rebuilding the affected games. Settle your pools before you generate the schedule. Tip: get pools right before you build the schedule. Pool assignment is the foundation the round-robin games and playoff seeds are built on — settling it first saves a rebuild later.

docs.text: Team Pool Assignment This is where you sort teams into divisions — the pools they play their round-robin games in. Like the Roster Swapper, it's two panels side by side: pick a division on the left and another on the right, then move teams between them. Divisions are grouped by age group in each picker. This is step 1 of the Scheduling Checklist, and the first thing to get right — nothing downstream can be built until every team is out of Unassigned . The arrow beside the title takes you back to the checklist. A division is a pool. How you split teams here decides who plays whom in pool play — and it feeds scheduling and bracket seeding downstream. Nothing can be scheduled out of Unassigned . New teams land in an Unassigned division until you place them. The builder has no pairing pattern for that division, so it silently skips those teams — which is why the Scheduling Checklist blocks the build until every age group is fully pooled. Emptying Unassigned is the goal of this screen. Moving teams Choose the two divisions you're balancing — one in each panel. Select teams in either panel and transfer them toward the other side. It works both directions. Use Filter teams… and the sortable columns to find teams quickly on a crowded division. Preview before you commit Moves go through a Transfer Preview first, so you can see exactly what's about to happen — including any Club Rep Impact — before confirming. Two outcomes are possible: Transfer A straight move — the team leaves one division and joins the other. Symmetrical swap When the target division is full, the preview asks you to send a team back the other way, so both pools stay within size. Balancing the pools The team rows carry ranking columns — for lacrosse events, national rank, rating, and record — so you can spread strong teams across pools instead of stacking them in one. Sort by rank to see the balance at a glance before you move anyone. Common mistakes Unbalanced pools. Dropping all the top teams into one division makes for a lopsided event — use the ranking columns to spread them. Ignoring the preview. The preview is where a simple move turns out to need a swap, or flags a club-rep impact. Read it before confirming. Reorganizing pools after scheduling. Divisions drive the games and the seeds — moving teams after games are built means rebuilding. Get pools right first.

docs.title: Push Notification
headings: Push Notification
Who receives a push notification?
Why is the device count lower than my registrant count?
How long should the message be?
Can I edit or recall a push after sending?
Did my last push go out?
docs.text: Push Notification Every push interrupts every device — there's no way to un-send it. Read it twice before you click Send. It goes to all mobile users at once, immediately. Who receives a push notification? Everyone using this event's mobile app who has notifications turned on. The device count at the top of the page is your live reach — that's exactly how many phones the next push will hit. Why is the device count lower than my registrant count? Push only reaches people who installed the mobile app and allowed notifications — that's always a subset of everyone registered. For full coverage, pair an urgent push with an email or bulletin so people without the app still get the word. How long should the message be? One short line. Phones truncate long push text, so lead with the essential fact — "Fields closed, games delayed to 2pm" beats a full paragraph nobody sees the end of. Can I edit or recall a push after sending? No. Once sent, it's on people's phones. If you made a mistake, send a brief follow-up correction rather than trying to undo the first one. Did my last push go out? Check the Sent Push Notifications list below the form — it shows every push newest-first with the sender, time, device count, and text. If it's there, it sent. Tip: save push for genuinely urgent, everyone-affected news — weather, delays, field moves. Overuse trains people to swipe your alerts away, and then the one that matters gets ignored too.

docs.title: Push Notification
headings: Push Notification
Sending one
History
Common mistakes
docs.text: Push Notification Send a short alert straight to the phones of everyone running your event's mobile app. Unlike email, a push pops up on the device immediately — use it for time-sensitive, everyone-needs-to-know moments like a weather delay, a field change, or "games resume in 15 minutes." A push goes to every registered device at once. There's no audience picker — it reaches all mobile users for this event. Send it only for things that truly concern everyone. Sending one Check the device count at the top — that's how many phones will receive the message right now. Type a short message in the Push Text box. Keep it to a sentence — push alerts truncate, and long ones lose their punch. Click Send Push Notification . You'll get a confirmation, and the box clears. History Every push you've sent is listed below the form — newest first — with who sent it, when, the device count at the time, and the text. Use it to confirm a message went out and to avoid sending duplicates. Common mistakes Writing a paragraph. Push text should be one short line; anything longer gets cut off on the device. Using it for routine info. A push interrupts everyone's phone — for non-urgent updates use a bulletin or email instead. Expecting it to reach people without the app. Only devices that installed the event's mobile app and opted into notifications receive a push — the device count is your real reach.

headings: QA Results
What's the difference between an error and a warning here?
It says a team is double-booked. How do I fix that?
QA flagged a rank mismatch or bracket error. Where do I go?
The game-count summary shows teams with different numbers of games. Is that an error?

docs.text: QA Results Errors must be fixed; warnings must be read. A red error stops play or breaks a bracket. A yellow warning may be fine — but "team has zero games" often isn't. Don't publish without checking both. What's the difference between an error and a warning here? Errors are things that break the event — a field or team booked twice at once, a seeding rank mismatch, a broken bracket — and must be fixed. Warnings are things to review, like a team with no games, back-to-back games, or repeated matchups; some are fine for your event, some aren't. It says a team is double-booked. How do I fix that? That team is scheduled for two games in the same slot. Move one of them in the Rescheduler , or rebuild the division on the hub's Schedule segment — one click away on the segment control. QA only reports the clash; resolve it there, then come back and re-run. QA flagged a rank mismatch or bracket error. Where do I go? Those come from playoff seeding. Open Bracket Seeds and check that each slot's Seed Pool and Seed Rank point at a position that pool can actually produce. Correct the seed, then re-run QA. The game-count summary shows teams with different numbers of games. Is that an error? Not necessarily — the balance summaries are informational, for fairness. Some formats legitimately give teams different counts. Use them to judge whether the spread is acceptable for your event, not as a blocker. I fixed the issues. Do I need to run QA again? Yes. QA reflects the schedule as it was at the last check. After any move or rebuild, re-run it to confirm the fix worked and nothing new was introduced. Everything says "All checks passed." Am I done? The structural checks are clean — no double-bookings, no broken brackets, no unscheduled active teams. That's the green light to publish. It's still worth a final human glance at the Master Schedule — the next segment along — but QA has cleared the errors that are hard to catch by eye. I opened this from the checklist and landed in the Schedule hub. Is that right? Yes. QA is one of the hub's four segments, so the checklist's QA Results tool opens the hub with QA already selected. Nothing is missing — every check, and the stats, are exactly the same. The point is that fixing what QA finds is a click away rather than a navigation. Tip: make QA the last step before every publish. It's the cheapest place to catch a double-booked team or a mis-seeded bracket — far cheaper than a coach catching it on game day.

After you build, it runs a comprehensive set of checks and tells you whether the schedule is clean, has warnings worth a look, or has hard errors you must fix before publishing. Three levels of finding Errors Things that break the event — a field or team booked twice at once, a seeding rank mismatch, a broken bracket. Fix these. Warnings Things to review — a team with no games, back-to-back games, repeated matchups, an inactive team still in a game. Summaries Balance checks — games per team, game spread, field utilization. Informational, for fairness. The critical checks (must-fix) Field double bookings — two games on the same field at the same time. Team double bookings — a team scheduled to play two games at once. Rank mismatches — a bracket seed pointing at a rank the pool can't produce. Bracket structural errors — a playoff bracket that doesn't hang together. These are the ones that stop play or produce a wrong bracket — clear them before publishing. Warnings worth a look Unscheduled teams — active teams with zero games. Almost always a real problem. Reading and acting on it The top badge shows the overall verdict and a total issue count; expand any section to see the specific games. QA only reports — you fix issues where they live: rebuild or delete on the hub's Schedule segment, move a game in the Rescheduler , or correct seeding in Bracket Seeds . Because QA is a segment rather than a separate page, the fix and the re-check are one click apart. Re-run QA to confirm it's clean. Common mistakes Publishing on warnings without reading them. A warning like "team has zero games" is often a genuine miss. Treating summaries as errors. Uneven game counts may be expected; they're there for fairness, not to block you. Not re-running after a fix. QA reflects the last build — re-run it once you've made changes.

docs.text: Quick Links Families can't register? Check the switch here first. These toggles decide whether registration and other paths appear on the public page — an "off" switch is the usual reason a button is missing. How do I set Quick Links for Player and Coach Self-Rostering? Self-rostering means the team registers first , then players and coaches attach themselves to a team that already exists. So the order matters — turn these on in sequence: Make sure teams exist. Both paths attach a person to a team, so with no teams there is nothing to join. Either add teams yourself, or run Register Team first and let club reps create them. Turn on Allow Player Self-Rostering . Turn on Allow Coach Registration . On tournament events, turn on Rosters (public access) so club reps, coaches, directors, recruiters and families can see who's on each team. Only a player's name, position and uniform number are displayed — nothing else. Coaches are listed on the rosters as well. The two switches you're after look like this once they're on: Allow Player Self-Rostering Players can self-roster onto a team — the "Self-Roster Player" Smart Bulletin shows on the landing page. On Allow Coach Registration Coaches can register and request teams — the "Register Coach" Smart Bulletin shows on the landing page. On Switched on but nothing appears on the public page? Coach registration warns you when no teams exist yet — the switch still saves, but the "Register Coach" Smart Bulletin stays hidden until teams are added. Add the teams and it appears on its own; you don't need to re-flip anything. On a league event the same switch reads Allow Player Registration rather than Self-Rostering, but it does the same thing — leagues don't register teams, so players always self-roster onto the teams you've built. What do these switches actually do? Each one shows or hides a Smart Bulletin on your event's public landing page — player registration, team registration, coach sign-up, store, and the like. On makes it appear to visitors; off retires it. Do I need to save after flipping a switch? No — each toggle saves on its own the instant you flip it, and the change is live on the public page right away. There's no separate Save button, so treat every flip as immediate. Why is one of the switches greyed out? A switch with a "SuperUser only" lock badge is TSIC-managed (insurance, store) — the state shown is real, but changing it is ours; contact us. Switches that don't apply to your event type at all simply don't appear on the list. (Rows also disable briefly while a flip is saving.) A switch showed a warning when I turned it on. Did it fail? No — the warning is a heads-up about a consequence (like opening coach registration before any teams exist), not a block. If that's intentional, leave it on; the switch still saved. Are these the same settings as in Configure Job? Yes. The same flags live in their proper Configure Job tabs; this screen just collects the public-facing ones in one place for speed. Change it here or there — it's the same setting. Tip: when a registration window closes, come here and switch that path off. It's the cleanest way to stop new sign-ups without editing dates or fees.

docs.text: Quick Links Your public home page now runs itself. There is nothing to remember, post, or take down — ever. You declare intent with a switch; the Smart Bulletins do the rest. These switches are the only moving part you own. These are the master switches for what your event's public home page offers. They drive the auto-updating Smart Bulletins visitors see — flip a switch and the public page changes, no publishing step. It's the fastest place to open or close registration and features for the event. The old way Hand-written bulletins you had to remember to post when registration opened, update when details changed, and take down when it closed — with a stale "Registration is open!" greeting visitors whenever you forgot. With Smart Bulletins Bulletins appear when everything's actually ready, tease "coming soon" while you set up, rewrite themselves when your configuration changes, and retire on their own when a window closes or the event concludes. Each switch saves the moment you flip it. There's no separate save — a toggle is live immediately, so a switch you turn off vanishes from the public page right away. If a save fails, the switch snaps back and a toast tells you. Every switch is a Smart Bulletin Each row here owns one Smart Bulletin on the public landing page: Register Team ON Registration Links TEAM Register Team Same pairing for every row: the player switch adds the Player link to that Smart Bulletin, View Schedule surfaces the "Game Schedules" Smart Bulletin, Store the "Merch Store" Smart Bulletin, and so on. The public page rebuilds itself from these flags on every visit — which is why the Smart Bulletins are "smart": nobody maintains them. One Smart Bulletin, three states A registration Smart Bulletin isn't simply visible or not — there's a state in between, and it works for you: Registration Links PLAYER Register Player Player Registration Coming soon — stay tuned! Coming Soon No Smart Bulletin Nothing on the landing page mentions this action at all. Live — switch on, everything ready: the full Smart Bulletin with its action button. Coming Soon — the switch is off , but the event has its registration set up (player profile built). The public page teases it automatically, so families know it's on the way before you open the doors. Gone — nothing configured, nothing promised: the Smart Bulletin doesn't exist. So "off" is not always invisible — an event mid-setup advertises itself. That's deliberate. Info Smart Bulletins — no switch of their own Not every Smart Bulletin has a row on this page. The info Smart Bulletins assemble themselves from your event's setup and ride along with the switches you do have. The best example — the USA Lacrosse membership notice: BEFORE YOU REGISTER USA Lacrosse Membership Required Name & date of birth match. Family Account details must match USA Lacrosse records exactly. Membership stays active. Must not expire before December 31, 2025 . Age verification complete. USA Lacrosse's one-time age verification. Look up your number Get or renew a membership Age verification It appears on its own when two things are true: player registration is open (your switch), and the player profile requires a USA Lacrosse membership number (your registration setup). The deadline it quotes is your configured validation window — change the setup and the Smart Bulletin rewrites itself; close registration and it retires with the registration Smart Bulletin. That's the pattern for info Smart Bulletins generally: they exist to answer a family's question before it becomes your support call, and their content is derived from configuration — you never author or maintain them. Switch ON but no Smart Bulletin? Five clauses decide Your switch is one vote of five. The public "Register Player" Smart Bulletin only shows when all of these pass: The event isn't over No newer edition of this event has replaced it The registration switch is on (this page) Fees are configured A team is open for players to join One ✗ anywhere and the Smart Bulletin stays hidden — with your switch honestly ON. The same is true for warnings you'll see right here on some rows: coach registration with no teams built yet, View Schedule with no games entered. The Smart Bulletin appears by itself the moment the missing fact exists. Tip: the live version of this checklist — with real dates, counts, and a fix link per failing line — sits on the Configure Job registration tabs. It's the server's own evaluation, so it can't disagree with what the public page is doing. Reading the rows The tip line states the current truth. Under every switch, the small line rewords itself for the position the switch is in — ON: "Teams can register — the 'Register Team' Smart Bulletin shows on the landing page." OFF: "Team registration is closed — the Smart Bulletin is hidden." Read the line, not just the switch. Locked switches are TSIC-managed. RegSaver insurance (player and team) and the Store carry a SuperUser only badge — the state shown is real; the flip just isn't yours. Ask us to change them. Labels adapt to your event type. A tournament registers teams and players join one, so its switch reads "Allow Player Self-Rostering " where a league's reads "Allow Player Registration ." Switches that can't apply to your event type simply don't appear — a shorter list means those actions aren't part of this event's shape. Same flags, one convenient place These switches also live in their proper Configure Job tabs — this screen just gathers the public-facing ones in one spot for quick access. Changing one here is the same as changing it there. Common mistakes Registration "isn't working" — but the switch is off. If families can't register, check that its toggle is on here first. This is the most common cause. Leaving a path open too long. A switch left on keeps accepting sign-ups; turn it off when a registration window closes. Expecting a locked switch to flip. The lock badge means the setting is TSIC-managed for your event — contact us rather than clicking harder.

docs.text: Referee Assignment Import your officials before you assign. The grid can only place referees who are already in your pool — load them first via CSV. How do I add my referees? Use the CSV File import to load your whole list of officials at once. After importing, they're available to assign to any game on the grid. How is the grid laid out? Fields run across the top and time slots down the side, so each cell is the game at that field and time. Use the day, time, age-group, and field filters to narrow it to the games you're staffing right now. Do I have to assign the same crew game by game? No. Copy a crew from one game to others, or bulk-assign a referee down a field's day by setting a Number of Timeslots , a Skip Interval , and a Direction — that places them across consecutive games in one action. How do I avoid double-booking a referee? Watch the grid as you assign — a referee placed on two games in the same timeslot is a conflict. Bulk assignment and crew-copy are quick, so scan the affected column afterward to confirm no one landed on overlapping games. Where can I see each referee's own schedule? Use the Referee Calendar for a per-official, game-by-game view of what each one is assigned. This screen is for making assignments; the calendar is the readable schedule of the result. Tip: staff one field's full day at a time. Filtering to a single field makes gaps obvious and lets you assign a crew straight down its timeslots without hopping around the grid.

docs.text: Registration Nothing is charged, and no one is registered, until you confirm payment. Everything before that step is safe to explore, back out of, and redo. Is my player registered before I pay? No. Move Back and Next through the steps as much as you like — the player is registered only once you confirm payment on the final step. How do I read the progress bar? A finished step turns green with a check; the step you're on is highlighted: Player → 2. Details → 3. Waivers → 4. Pay I closed the browser partway through. Did I lose everything? No. Progress is saved as you go, so you can return and pick up where you left off. Since nothing is final until payment, an unfinished registration just waits for you. Why is the "Continue" button greyed out? A step still needs something — a required field, or a waiver not yet accepted. The step points out what's missing; once it's handled, the button turns active: Continue to payment Can I go back and fix an earlier step? Yes — use Back anytime. A green check means the step is complete, not locked. Nothing is committed until you confirm payment. How do I register more than one player? Finish this player all the way through, then start the wizard again for the next. Each player is registered separately. What's the difference between the deposit and the full price? When the event allows it, the payment step offers a smaller deposit to hold the spot now, with the balance due later. If there's no deposit option, you pay the full amount. Can I pay in installments instead of all at once? On events that offer it, the payment step lets you either pay in full at registration or set up automatic payments (an installment plan). If you choose automatic payments, the fee is split into a set number of equal monthly installments: The first payment is charged the day after you register. The remaining payments are charged automatically once a month from that first date, until the balance is paid. You'll receive a receipt each time a payment is processed. If an event doesn't show an automatic-payment option, it isn't offered for that registration. How do I update my card — or pay a missed installment — on automatic payments? While your plan is still running , both are the same screen: updating your card also settles anything past due, so you don't need to pay separately first. If your automatic payments have already stopped, use "Pay Balance Due" instead. Once a plan has been cancelled or has come to an end, there's no longer a card on file to update — so the menu offers Pay Balance Due rather than Update CC Info. It takes a card and settles what's owed in one payment. Sign in — from the upper right of your event's home page, or at teamsportsinfo.com. Choose your player's role — the one with automatic payments set up. Open the User Menu in the upper right and select Update CC Info . Fill in the Update Payment Method form and click Update Card & Pay Balance . Have more than one player? Use Switch Role in the same menu to select each additional player and repeat — every player's subscription holds its own card. The User Menu, with the item you want: My Registration Update CC Info Select this Check My Email Switch Role Use this for your other players The form that opens: Balance Due 0.00 Your player, event, and subscription number appear here. Cardholder name, billing address, ZIP, and email Card number, CVV, expiration month and year XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Update Card & Pay Balance Check Balance Due at the top of that form before you submit — it tells you what the button will charge: 0.00 — you're up to date. Nothing is charged; the new card is simply stored for future installments. Any other amount — that's a missed installment, and it's charged when you click the button. Don't see "Update CC Info" in the menu? It appears only for a player whose automatic payments are currently running . Three reasons it might be missing: this player was never on a plan; the plan has ended or been cancelled (look for Pay Balance Due instead); or you're signed in under a different player — try Switch Role . If the page won't cooperate: Confirm you're on the right event and the right player before entering card details. Try a different browser, or a different device. On a phone? Try a computer. Avoid school or work devices — their firewalls often block payment forms. Tip: if a price, date, or required field looks wrong, don't guess — the league contact on the event's landing page would rather answer a quick question than untangle it later.

Why is the schedule grid blank when I open the page? By design — the Rescheduler waits for you to filter to the games you want before loading anything. If the slot you need doesn't exist, use Add Timeslot to create a row at a specific date and time first. A whole day got pushed back by weather. Do I move every game? No — use the weather adjustment . Set a New First Game Time and the day's games shift together to the later start, so one action re-times the entire day instead of dozens of manual moves. It warned me about a time clash. What does that mean? The slot you're moving into would put a team in two places at once — one of its games already sits in that timeslot. The warning is your cue to pick a different slot before you commit the move. How do the teams find out a game moved? Send them a note from here: fill in the Subject and Message Body to dispatch a schedule-change notification to the affected teams. Moving the game and notifying are separate actions — do both so nobody shows up at the old time. Should I build a new schedule here? No. The Rescheduler is for moving games that already exist. To generate games, rebuild a division, or delete a build, use the Schedule Hub . Tip: filter down to the single day or field you're changing before you start moving games. A tight grid makes the open slots obvious and keeps you from dropping a game into the wrong division.

Moving and swapping games Select a game, then drop it on an open slot to move it. Drop it on another game to swap the two. Need a slot that doesn't exist yet? docs.text: Roster Swapper Every swap commits immediately — there's no separate save. Each move reassigns the player right away, so double-check the player and the two teams before you swap. Which way does a swap go? Toward the other panel. The control on the Source Team roster sends selected players to the Target Team , and the control on the Target roster sends them back to the Source. Set both team pickers first so you're moving between the two you intend. Can I move several players at once? Yes — select multiple players in a roster and swap them together as a batch. Use the Filter players… box and the sortable columns to pick out the right people first. What does the n/n badge on each team mean? It's current roster over the team's maximum — e.g. 14/18 means 14 players on an 18-cap team. Watch it while moving players in so you don't overfill a team. How do I get a player onto a team who isn't on one yet? Pick the Unassigned pool as your source, select the person, and swap them to the target team. To take someone off a team without deleting their registration, do the reverse — swap them into the Unassigned pool. A coach asked to join a team but isn't showing on the roster. Why? Coach team requests have to be approved first. Open the Coach Approvals queue (linked from this screen's header) to review and approve them. The Requests and Role columns here show who's requested or assigned to coach each team. I moved a player by mistake. How do I undo it? There's no undo button — just swap them back. Set the team they landed on as the source, select the player, and send them to their original team. Because moves are live, correcting one is the same action in reverse. Tip: when rebalancing two teams, put one as Source and the other as Target and work entirely between those two panels — you can move players each way without re-picking teams between swaps.

docs.text: Roster Swapper Move players from one team to another. The screen is two side-by-side rosters — a Source Team on the left and a Target Team on the right. Pick a team on each side, select the players you want to move, and swap them across. A swap is a real roster change. The player is reassigned immediately — it affects their team, their schedule, and their coach's roster. Move the right player to the right team. How to move players Choose a team in the Source Team picker and another in Target Team . Select one or more players in either roster, then use the swap control to send them to the other side. It works both directions — Source → Target and Target → Source — so you can rebalance two teams without leaving the screen. Selecting several players and swapping them together does the move in one batch. Reading the roster count Each panel shows a roster / max badge (e.g. 14/18 ) — current players over the team's cap. Watch it as you move players in so you don't push a team past its limit. Use the Filter players… box and the sortable columns to find someone quickly on a long roster. The "Unassigned" pool Staff and players who aren't on a team yet live in an Unassigned pool. Pick it as your source to place people onto teams, or as your target to pull someone off a team without deleting their registration. Coaches and team requests Coaches can request to be added to teams; those don't take effect until approved. The Coach Approvals queue (linked from the header) is where you review and approve them — the Requests and Role columns here show who's coaching what. Common mistakes Swapping the wrong direction. Confirm which side is Source and which is Target before you move — the button on each roster sends players toward the opposite panel. Overfilling a team. Keep an eye on the roster/max badge; moving players in can exceed the cap. Treating it like a draft board. Every swap is live — there's no separate "save," so each move is committed as you make it.

How do I get to this screen?

A tile is highlighted and says teams are without a game. What now?
