docs.text: Schedule Dashboard This screen reports; it doesn't change anything. Read what the build produced here, then fix it on the Scheduling Checklist or the Schedule hub. How do I get to this screen? Click the stat band under the title on the Scheduling Checklist — the row showing the date span, fields, and divisions. The arrow beside this page's title takes you back. It says "No games scheduled yet." The schedule hasn't been built. Everything on this page is a summary of existing games, so there's nothing to show until the build has run. Work the Scheduling Checklist steps first. A tile is highlighted and says teams are without a game. What now? The build couldn't place them. The usual causes, in order of likelihood: those teams are still in the Unassigned pool; their pool has no timeslots on a day the age group plays; or there simply weren't enough open slots. The Scheduling Checklist catches the first two by name — start there, then re-build. Worth knowing: a build that can't place everything doesn't fail, it just places less. These tiles are the honest count of what came up short. Why are fewer fields in use than I assigned to the event? Assigning a field to the event only makes it available . It gets games only if it's also ticked for a day in Assign Timeslots . A field with no timeslots is invisible to the builder. Play days and the date span don't match. Is that wrong? No — they're different measures. The span is first game date to last; play days counts the days that actually have games. A Friday–Sunday event that doesn't play Saturday shows a three-day span and two play days. Both numbers are true. One day has far more games than the others. Usually the light days are short on timeslots rather than the heavy day being over-booked — the builder puts games where slots exist. Open Assign Timeslots for the age groups involved and compare the days. Is this the same as QA? No, and they're complementary. This page reports what's missing — teams and divisions with no games. QA reports what clashes — a team booked twice, a field double-used, a broken bracket. Run both before you publish. Tip: check this page immediately after every build, before you look at any grid. Two highlighted tiles here take ten seconds to read and will save you finding the same gap by eye an hour later.

docs.text: Schedule Dashboard A one-screen read on the schedule you've built: how big it is, how it spreads across the days, and — the part worth looking at — what got left out . Open it by clicking the stat band under the title on the Scheduling Checklist ; the arrow beside the title brings you back. It fills in after the build. Before there are games there is nothing to summarize — readiness is the only status that matters, and the Scheduling Checklist is where that lives. The tiles Games Total games on the books for the event. Play days Distinct days with games, plus the first-to-last date span beneath. A weekend event with a gap shows both numbers honestly. Fields in use How many fields the build actually put games on — which can be fewer than you assigned. Divisions scheduled Shown as scheduled / schedulable when any division came up short, with the shortfall named underneath. Teams scheduled Shown as scheduled / active when any active team has no game at all. A highlighted tile means something was skipped. "3 divisions without games" or "12 teams without a game" is the build telling you it couldn't place them — usually missing timeslots on a day, teams still in Unassigned , or not enough field capacity. A build that skips work does not fail; it just builds less. These two tiles are how you notice. Games per day A bar per play day, so you can see the shape of the event at a glance. A day carrying far more games than the others usually means the other days are short on timeslots — worth a look in Assign Timeslots before anyone tries to play it. Where to act on what you see Teams or divisions without games — check pools and timeslots on the Scheduling Checklist , then re-build on the Schedule hub. Fewer fields in use than expected — a field with no timeslots for a day gets no games, even though it's assigned to the event. Conflicts, not counts — that's QA , not this screen. This one tells you what's missing; QA tells you what clashes.

docs.text: Schedule Hub If the Build button won't run, the event isn't fully configured yet. Pools, dates, timeslots, and pairings all have to be in place first — the setup check tells you which one is missing, and the Scheduling Checklist tracks the same list as steps. Where do I start on a brand-new event? On the Scheduling Checklist , not here — it walks you through pooling teams, setting play dates and timeslots, and only then sends you to this screen to build. Within the hub, Configure pulses Start here when the event has no games; that's where the dates, fields, rules, and waves the builder reads all live. What's the difference between the Schedule and Master segments? Schedule is your working surface — you build and place games there, scoped to the event, an age group, or a single division. Master is the read view of the entire event on one grid: what players, coaches, and referees ultimately see, and where you export to Excel. I clicked QA Results on the checklist and landed here instead. Why? Because QA is a segment of this screen. Rather than maintain two versions of QA and Master with different chrome around them, the checklist's tools open the hub with the right segment already selected. Nothing is missing — the exports, the stats, and every check are all here. I clicked Build but it only rebuilt one division. Why? Build acts on the scope you have selected in the left navigator. If you're drilled into a division, the button reads Build / Re-Build for that division only — and it prints the scope name right on the button. Click Event at the top of the navigator to build everything at once. Can I just build one age group at a time and work through the event? Don't. Every age group is competing for the same field-hours, and the builder only knows about the demand in the scope you gave it — an age group built first will take the slots it likes with no idea what still has to fit around it. Build at Event scope, then use a single age group or division build to repair one piece afterwards. It says the setup check needs pairings. Do I have to go set them up? No — the Setup incomplete panel has a button that generates the missing pool sizes for you. Open Manage Pairings only if you want to review or customize the who-plays-whom pattern before generating. My round-robin games built, but the championship games are missing. That's expected — round-robin (pool) games generate automatically, but championship and bracket games are placed by hand so you control which slot each one lands in. The hub moves you to the affected division and shows a banner. Use Add Row to open a timeslot at the right time, then drop each game onto it. I don't want to place the championship games yet. Park them. Parking moves the championship games into a collapsible Parking section at the bottom of the grid and frees the timeslots they were holding. Expand it and drag them back individually when you're ready to place them for real. Can I place games with the keyboard instead of dragging? Yes. Switch to keyboard placement and clicking a game opens Rapid Placement , where you type to pick a field and a time. Prefer the mouse? Leave it on mouse mode and click the game, then click the open slot. Your preference is saved. How do I clear a schedule and start over? Delete acts on the selected scope — a single division , an age group , or (at event scope) the whole build. Deleting frees those games' timeslots so you can rebuild. Because it's scope-aware, double-check the scope label before you confirm. This is a returning event — do I still need to touch Configure? Yes. The hub carries last year's fields, dates, and waves forward for you, which saves the typing but is still a guess: it can't know that you took 40 more teams this year, or dropped a field. Every setting the builder reads is on one of the Configure tabs, and Config Summary shows them all in a single table for a fast review. It's telling me I need pools or bracket seeds. Where are those? Both open inside the hub from Configure , alongside Manage Fields, Manage Pairings and Assign Timeslots. Pool Assignment sorts teams within an age group into pools; Bracket Seeds sets the playoff seeding. Use the Back button in the toolbar to return to the segment you came from. Why does it say I need a desktop? The scheduling grid relies on drag-and-drop and precise placement that don't work well on a phone or small tablet. Open this screen on a laptop or desktop for the full experience. Tip: always run QA before you publish. It catches the conflicts that are hard to spot by eye — a team booked twice in one slot, a field double-used — while they're still cheap to fix. It's one click away on the segment control.

headings: Schedule Hub

Common mistakes
If you get stuck
docs.text: Schedule Hub This is where the schedule gets built and managed. You arrive here from the Schedule button on step 4 of the Scheduling Checklist — the arrow at the top-left takes you back. The hub has three segments in one control at the top; each is a different job on the same event, and you move between them freely rather than in a fixed order. Use a desktop. The grid, drag-and-drop, and game placement need a full-size screen — the hub asks for a desktop browser rather than a phone or small tablet. The three segments Schedule The working surface. Build games for the selected scope, then place any championship/bracket games onto the grid by hand. QA Conflict checks — a team double-booked, a field clash, a broken bracket — to run before you publish. Master The whole event on one grid — the view everyone else consumes, and where you export to Excel. QA and Master are also listed as tools on the Scheduling Checklist. Those links land you right here on the matching segment — same screen, same chrome, whichever door you came through. Setup lives on the checklist, not here Everything the build reads — fields, pools, play dates, timeslots — is authored through the Scheduling Checklist steps before you arrive. The hub's setup check verifies it all again at build time and names anything missing. Game guarantees and placement rules are reviewed in the build flow itself. Scope: Event, Age Group, or Division In Schedule mode the navigator on the left lets you work at three levels. Build and delete always act on the scope you've selected: Event → Age Group → Division The Build button always names the current scope and reads Re-Build once that scope already has games. The scope you're in is shown in the breadcrumb above the grid. Build the whole event first; build one division only to repair it. Placing games is a contention problem — every age group is competing for the same field-hours. A full-event build sees all of that demand at once. Building a single division early lets it grab slots with no knowledge of what still has to fit, and you find out at the end. Single-scope builds are a repair tool for after a full build, not a way to work through the event a pool at a time. Building the games In Schedule mode, click Build (or Re-Build ) to auto-generate round-robin games for the selected scope. A setup check runs first and, if anything is missing, lists it in a Setup incomplete panel — missing pairings can be generated right from that panel. Championship / bracket games are placed by hand. After the round-robin build the hub switches you to the affected division and shows a banner — use Add Row to create a timeslot at the right interval, then drop each championship game onto it. Two placement styles: mouse (click a game, click an open slot) or keyboard (Rapid Placement — type a field and a time). Your choice is remembered. Not ready to place a championship game yet? Park it. Parked games move to the collapsible Parking section at the bottom of the grid and free their timeslots; drag them back individually when you are. Common mistakes Building before setup is done. If the setup check blocks you, the panel names what's missing. Fields, dates, timeslots, and pools are the usual culprits — and the Scheduling Checklist tracks all of them. Building at the wrong scope. Check the scope name on the Build button — it's easy to rebuild one division when you meant the whole event, or vice-versa. Walking away with championship games unplaced. Round-robin games build automatically; bracket games don't. If the banner is up, you still have games to place. If you get stuck Run QA before publishing — it surfaces conflicts you can't easily eyeball. If a build won't start, the setup-incomplete panel tells you exactly what's missing, and the Scheduling Checklist (back arrow, top-left) shows the same gaps as a work list.

docs.text: Scheduling Checklist Work the steps top to bottom. Each step links to the screen that turns it green, and every one of those screens has a back arrow to here. When fields, pools, play dates and timeslots are green, Build unlocks. Where did the rest of the Scheduling menu go? It's all here. The menu used to list eleven scheduling screens with no indication of which ones you still needed; now there's one Scheduling Checklist item, and this page routes you to everything — steps at the top, tools below. Every screen it opens has a back arrow to return here. Why is Build Schedule locked? One of the steps it depends on isn't finished, and the row names them: "Locked until complete: fields, pools, play dates, timeslots" . The most common blocker is teams still sitting in the Unassigned pool — those teams can never be placed in a schedule, so the build stays locked until every age group is fully pooled. What does the detail line under a step mean? It's the live list of what's missing. "2029: 12 of 59" under Pools means that age group still has 12 unpooled teams out of 59. "No play dates: 2030" means that age group has no game dates. "4 pools without timeslots — 2030: White, Red" names the individual pools. Fix exactly what's named and the step turns green. Play dates and timeslots are one step. Which is which? They're set on the same screen but at different grains. Play dates belong to the age group — 2030 plays Saturday and Sunday. Timeslots belong to the pool — you set up 2030 Red, then 2030 White. Step 3 reports both, so a green age group can still show individual pools missing timeslots. Pairings shows missing pool sizes. Do I have to fix that? No — pairings are informational and never block the build. Any missing pool size is generated automatically when the build runs. Open the Pairings screen only if you want to review or customize who-plays-whom beforehand. It mentions divisions without a game guarantee. Is that blocking me? No. If a division has no guarantee set, the builder works one out from the pairing table and writes it back. The note exists so you know it's being derived rather than chosen — if the derived number isn't what your event promises, set it explicitly on the hub's Build Rules tab before you build. I don't see a Bracket Seeds step. Then this event has no bracket games. The step only appears when there are playoff games to seed — showing a permanently green check for work that never applied would be a hollow claim. Bracket games are created during the build from championship pairings; once they exist, the step appears. Bracket Seeds is red but I've seeded everything I can see. A slot counts as covered if it has a seed ("Pool A #1") or an advancement feed — meaning it's filled by the winner or loser of an earlier bracket game. Later-round slots are usually fed, not seeded. The step lists the uncovered slots by age group and slot label, so open Bracket Seeds and look for exactly those. Why are the Tools grayed out? The Tools all operate on games — Master Schedule, Rescheduler, Schedule Viewer, QA Results and the rest — so they unlock once the schedule has been built. Until then the steps are the whole job. QA Results opened the Schedule hub instead of its own page. Is that right? Yes. QA Results and Master Schedule are segments of the Schedule hub, so their tools open the hub with that segment already selected — one door, one set of chrome. Everything on those screens works the same as it always did; the exports and stats are all still there. A step went from green back to red. What happened? The checklist reads live data, so something changed underneath it — new teams registered into an age group and landed in Unassigned , or a pool was added without timeslots. That's the point of it: it stays accurate all event long rather than recording that you once finished a step. Tip: for a returning event, the checklist is the fastest way to confirm what carried forward from last year. A glance tells you whether dates and timeslots are already green before you spend time in the configuration screens.

headings: Scheduling Checklist
The steps, in order
Reading a step
Tools — after the build
After a build, the header tells you what you built
Common mistakes
docs.text: Scheduling Checklist This is the front door to scheduling — the one Scheduling item in the menu, and the page every other scheduling screen sends you back to. It is an ordered list of the work that has to happen before a schedule can be built, with live status read from your actual data. Each step names exactly what is still missing — which age groups, which pools, which teams — and links straight to the screen that fixes it. Build stays locked until the steps above it are green. A season with no fields assigned, teams left in the Unassigned pool, age groups with no play dates, pools with no timeslots — the builder would silently skip all of them. The checklist blocks the build rather than let it produce a schedule that quietly leaves teams out. The steps, in order 0 · Set Up Fields The prerequisite, numbered zero on purpose: timeslots are built on fields, so the season needs its fields assigned before anything downstream means anything. Opens Manage Fields to pull this season's fields in from the shared pool (or create new ones). 1 · Assign Teams To Pools Every team moves out of Unassigned into a real pool. The detail line counts the unpooled teams and names the age groups holding them — "2029: 12 of 59". Opens Pool Assignment . 2 · Pairings Who plays whom, per pool size. Informational — it never blocks the build, because any missing pool size is generated automatically when the build runs. Visit it only to review or customize the pattern. 3 · Assign Timeslots Two things on one screen: the dates each age group plays and the field timeslots each pool gets on those days. The detail line reports both — "No play dates: 2030" and "4 pools without timeslots — 2030: White, Red". 4 · Build Schedule Unlocks once fields, pools, play dates and timeslots are green, then opens the Schedule hub to run the build. Once games exist the row turns green and shows the game count. 5 · Bracket Seeds (only when the event has bracket games) Every playoff slot needs either a seed ("Pool A #1") or an advancement feed (the winner of an earlier bracket game). The step counts the slots that have neither. It is hidden entirely on events with no bracket games. Reading a step The badge on the left is the step number while there's work left, and turns into a green check when the step is done. The line under the title is live data, not boilerplate. If it names an age group or a pool, that is the thing standing between you and a build. Build Schedule shows what is blocking it — "Locked until complete: pools, play dates" — so you never have to guess which step to go back to. Game guarantees don't block the build. If a division has no game guarantee set, the builder derives one from the pairing table and uses that. The Build step mentions the divisions in that position as a note, so you can set an explicit number on the hub's Build Rules tab if the derived one isn't what you want. Tools — after the build The Tools grid unlocks once games exist. These are the things you reach for over and over during an event; none of them is ever "finished", which is why none of them is a step: Master Schedule — the whole event on one grid. Rescheduler — move or swap individual games; rain-delay the whole day. Schedule Viewer — browse games, enter scores, check standings and brackets. Schedule Reports — printable game cards and team schedules. QA Results — conflict checks to run before you publish. Tournament Parking and Mobile Scorers — game-day logistics. Master Schedule and QA Results open inside the Schedule hub on their own segment, so the chrome around them stays the same wherever you came from. Every other tool opens on its own page with a back arrow to this checklist. After a build, the header tells you what you built Once games exist a stat band appears under the title: the date span and number of play days, the fields in use , and the divisions scheduled . The game count stays in the badge next to the page title. Before the build there is no band — readiness is the only status that matters, and that's the list itself. Common mistakes Treating a partially-red step as "close enough". One age group with unpooled teams blocks the entire build. The step names it — fix exactly that. Chasing the Pairings step. It is informational by design. Missing pool sizes are generated at build time; it will never unlock anything. Assuming last year carried forward. A returning event often has dates and timeslots already seeded from the prior year — the checklist tells you whether they actually landed. Trust the status, not the memory of setting it up. Not coming back. Pools change during registration. Re-check the checklist after roster or pool changes, not just before the first build.

docs.text: Pro tips Work that never appears as a step on the checklist — the prep that makes the steps go faster, and the craft that happens around them. Click any title to expand it. Before you pool Incorporate national rankings to assist pool assignment If you want pools built by strength rather than by guesswork, do this before step 1. USA Lacrosse › USA Lacrosse Rankings attaches published national ranking numbers to the teams registered in your event, and every number you save turns up as a sortable Nat'l column in Pool Assignment: Season National Rankings Agegroups Your event's Agegroups Find Matches Pool Assignment Team Nat'l Doing it first is the whole point: with the column populated you sort by rank and snake the top teams across pools, so the strong ones don't stack up in one bracket. Doing it after pools are set means re-doing the assignment you just finished. Two things to know going in. The ranking age groups are published by graduation class , so you pair each one with the age group in your event that holds those players — and for a new event, the most recently completed season is the one with a full year of results behind it. And the matcher is a best guess from club name, colour, grad year and state, so review every pairing, not just the weak ones; hand-matched teams are always saved regardless of the confidence level you pick. Tournaments only, and read live from a site we don't control. Matching registered teams exists to seed tournament pools, so it is offered on tournaments only — leagues can browse the published rankings but not attach them. The numbers are read live from usclublax.com, which can change or go offline, so check the results before you seed on them. Re-running is safe at any time: saving again overwrites. Quickly create pools and optionally theme your event Divisions are your pools, and their names follow the event everywhere — schedules, reports, the app. So settle them before you start moving teams. In Teams & Rosters › L-A-D-T Editor , the menu above the tree opens Theme Division Names : type one list of names and it applies to every age group at once — creating the divisions that do not exist yet and renaming the ones that do. Plain Pool A / Pool B / Pool C, or a theme for the tournament if you want one. Red White Blue 2029 A Red 2030 new Blue The panel underneath is a real dry run. Before you type it lists your Current Divisions ; as soon as there are names it becomes a Preview , age group by age group, showing each rename, each division it would create, and each one it would remove. Nothing happens until Apply Theme . A division holding teams is never removed. If your list is shorter than an age group's existing divisions, the surplus ones would be removed — but only while they're empty. Any division with teams in it shows as has teams in the preview and is left alone, so this is safe to run on an event that's already partly pooled.

docs.text: Searching registrations Filters don't apply until you press Search. Set your criteria, then press Search . Closing the drawer with unapplied changes prompts you to run it. I changed my filters but the results didn't update. Filters take effect only when you press Search . Active filters then show as removable chips above the results, so you can always see — and clear — what's applied. A filter changed the role for me. Is that a bug? No. A few filters narrow the role because they only make sense for one kind of registrant — an insurance filter implies players, for example. Some filters also appear only when the event uses that feature (RegSaver insurance, or ARB recurring billing). What do the red amount and calendar icon in the Owed column mean? $250 owed Auto-pay scheduled A red amount means a balance is due; a calendar icon means an automatic payment is scheduled for an upcoming date. The footer totals Paid and Owed across the whole result set. Why are some rows struck through? Those registrations are inactive . The strikethrough sets them apart from active rows. How do I email just some people, not everyone? Check the rows you want and use Email Selected to open the batch composer for those people. Email All composes to the entire result set. Where do I refund a card payment or delete a registration? Click a person's name to open their detail panel. From there you can update contact info and demographics, process a credit-card refund, or delete the registration. Why don't I see the Invite button? Two things have to be true. Your search must be scoped to a single invitable role — Player or Club Rep — since an invitation is tied to that role, and there must be another event you're eligible to invite them to. If either isn't the case, the button stays hidden. What does "Look up CCs expiring this month" do? For events with recurring billing, it queries the card processor live and returns everyone with a card about to expire — deliberately ignoring your current filters — so you can collect balances before an automatic payment fails. Tip: the filter chips above the results are your safety check. If a search looks wrong, check the chips before assuming the data is off — usually a stray filter is still applied.

The audience is re-resolved from your filter criteria at send time, so the headline count is the real total, not the visible page. Email Selected is exactly the rows you've checked — and checks accumulate across pages . Check three people on page 1, page ahead, check two more: the button reads "Email Selected (5)" and the composer lists all five by name. Pre-built email templates — the list adapts to your search The batch composer offers ready-made letters, but which ones appear depends on the job's features and what you searched. Scope the search to "ARB Behind — Active/Suspended" and the matching collections letter shows up, pre-written with the right instructions: Update CC Info (Active/Suspended) ARB — Behind in Payment Pay Balance Due (Expired/Terminated) ARB — Behind in Payment Tip: if a template you expect is missing, your search probably isn't scoped to its audience yet — the picker only offers letters that fit the people in your results. Email Tokens Anywhere you compose — the batch composer here, or a single registrant's Email tab — you can insert tokens that render as each recipient's real values at send time: !PERSON !EMAIL !FAMILYUSERNAME !JOBNAME !JOBLINK !AMTFEES !AMTPAID !AMTOWED !SEASON !SPORT !CUSTOMERNAME So "Your balance of !AMTOWED for !JOBNAME" personalizes itself for every recipient in one send. Events with recurring billing or USA Lacrosse validation get extra tokens (subscription ID and status, membership valid-through date) — they appear in the token list only where they apply. Invite all Players / Invite Club Reps Sends each recipient a signed, expiring invitation link into another of your events — no manual link-building. The button appears when two things are true: your search is narrowed to exactly one invitable role (Players or Club Reps), and another event under your organization currently has that registration type open. With rows checked, it flips to inviting just those people: Invite all Players → with 3 rows checked → Invite 3 checked Players You pick the target event and the invitation window; every email in the batch states the same deadline. Filter chips Every active filter shows as a removable chip above the results — what you see is always exactly what's applied: Role: Player × Status: Active × Agegroup: 2027 × Tree selections stay tidy: checking an agegroup covers every division and team under it but shows one chip, not fifty. Removing that chip un-checks the whole subtree in one click. Set Filters drawer Search by billing/payment properties The Billing section turns payment paperwork into search keys — paste an invoice number from a receipt or processor record and land on the registration behind it. Events with recurring billing can also search by subscription number or subscription status: ARB Subscription Invoice # Subscription # Search by Roster Size The Roster Scan section finds the clubs falling behind: "Rostered Players ≤ N" returns the Club Reps who own at least one team with that few active rostered players. Optionally scope it to specific clubs, then use Email All to nudge every rep in one pass: Rostered Players <= For Club Search for CC-Expiring Registrants In events with recurring billing, the ARB section has a button that isn't a filter — it's a live lookup at the card processor: Look up CCs expiring this month results arrive under a dedicated chip: ARB: CCs Expiring This Month (12) × It deliberately ignores your filters — even dropped or inactive registrants surface if their card is about to fail — so you can collect before an automatic payment bounces. The × on the chip exits the lookup and restores your normal filters untouched. Registrant detail panel Click any name to open the panel. It's divided into three tabs — money first, identity second, correspondence third: Accounting Details Email Accounting tab: refund, re-send confirmation, manage subscription Process a credit-card refund — refund directly from the accounting ledger; the record lands in the same ledger you're looking at. Re-Send Confirmation Email — one click re-sends the original registration confirmation. It's role-aware: for a player it sends the family confirmation to the family account. Manage the recurring-billing subscription — for ARB registrants the subscription card shows payment progress and can pull the live status from the processor on demand; a live, active subscription can be cancelled right here. The footer totals Paid and Owed across all results. Why is there a small dot next to some team names? That marks a team whose club rep has opted out of email — worth knowing before you try to reach them or send reminders. Why are team names shown as "Club: Team"? Yes — Export downloads the current results to Excel, exactly as filtered. docs.text: Store Admin Colors × sizes = SKUs. An item's sellable variations are generated automatically from the colors and sizes you attach. Get those lists right first, and the SKU matrix builds itself. What's a SKU, and where do they come from? A SKU is one sellable variation of an item — a specific color and size, like "Hoodie / Navy / Large." When you create an item and pick its colors and sizes, the store generates a SKU for every combination automatically. Expand an item to see them. How do I stop selling something without deleting it? Toggle it inactive . You can deactivate a whole item, or just one SKU (say, only the small size sold out). It disappears from the storefront but keeps its history and can be switched back on. Why won't it let me delete a color or size? Because a SKU still uses it — deleting would orphan that variation. Remove the color/size from the items that use it first, or simply leave it in place. Unused colors and sizes do no harm. What does "max can sell" do? It's your inventory cap. At the item level it limits total sales; at the SKU level it limits that specific color/size. Once a SKU hits its max, buyers can't order more of it — set these to what you actually have in stock. I added an item but it's not in the store. Why? Check three things: the item is active, it has at least one active SKU, and the store itself is enabled for the event. Any one of those being off will hide it from shoppers. Where do I see how sales are going? The Analytics tab. It summarizes store performance so you can see what's moving and what isn't without digging through orders. Tip: build your colors and sizes lists once, up front. After that, adding a new item is just naming it, pricing it, and ticking the variations it comes in — the SKUs handle themselves.

docs.text: Store Admin This is where you build and run your event's merchandise store — the items families can buy (spirit wear, add-ons, extras), the colors and sizes they come in, and the sales numbers behind them. It's organized into four tabs: Items , Colors , Sizes , and Analytics . How items and SKUs fit together An item is a product (say, "Event Hoodie") with a name, price, and description. When you create it, you pick which colors and sizes it comes in, and the store automatically generates a SKU for every combination — Navy/Small, Navy/Medium, Red/Small, and so on. Each SKU is what actually gets sold and stocked. Set up colors and sizes first. An item's SKU matrix is built from the colors and sizes you select — so define those on their tabs before creating items that use them. The tabs Items — add/edit products, set price and description, choose colors/sizes, and toggle an item active. Expand any item to see its SKUs and adjust each one's stock limit or turn individual SKUs off. Colors — the color options items can use. Add, rename, or remove them. Sizes — the size options items can use. Add, rename, or remove them. Analytics — what's selling, for reviewing store performance. Stock and availability Max-can-sell caps how many of an item (and each SKU) can be sold — your inventory ceiling. Active controls whether something appears in the storefront. Deactivate an item, or a single SKU, to pull it from sale without deleting it. Common mistakes Trying to delete a color or size that's in use. If a SKU uses it, the delete is blocked — retire it by removing it from items first, or just leave it. Forgetting an item is inactive. If a product isn't showing in the store, check that both it and its SKUs are active. Leaving max-can-sell at a placeholder. Set it to your real inventory so you don't oversell.

docs.text: Store — questions Do I need an account to shop? Usually you sign in with your family account. Some events also let you Continue as Guest and check out without one. If the store asks you to sign in first, that guest option — when available — is on the sign-in screen. Why do I have to choose a player before adding an item? When your account has registered players, the store asks who each item is for so it's tied to the right player. Pick the player and the name follows the item through your cart and checkout. A size shows "Sold out" or "Only a few left." Stock is live. Sold-out sizes are dimmed and can't be added, and low counts show how many remain. Choose another size or check back later. How do I pay, and can I use American Express? Checkout takes a credit card. Whether American Express is accepted depends on the event's payment settings — if it's not allowed, use another card. What is "Stay-to-Play"? It's an alternate menu label that opens the same event store. When your event uses it, any lodging options appear among the store items — there's no separate booking screen here. Can I get a receipt? Yes. The order confirmation shows your order number, total paid, and transaction reference, with a Download Receipt button for a PDF. The store is empty or won't open. "No items available right now" means nothing's currently for sale for this event. If the store is turned off entirely, it simply won't appear in your menu — check back closer to the event.

docs.text: Team Links These links show up on player-facing team pages. Anything you add here is visible to the families of the team you assign it to — so post only links you're happy for them to see. Where do these links appear? On your event's player-facing team pages. A link assigned to a specific team appears on that team's page; a link set to — All Teams — appears for everyone. What's the difference between one team and All Teams? Pick a single team for something that only concerns them (their practice schedule). Pick — All Teams — for event-wide resources everyone should have (the venue map, the event rules page). All-Teams links save you from adding the same link to every team one by one. My link doesn't open, or goes to the wrong place. Why? Almost always the URL. Edit the link and make sure it starts with https:// and is the complete address — copy it straight from your browser's address bar rather than typing it by hand. I deleted a link by mistake — can I get it back? There's no undo, but re-adding it takes seconds: click Add, pick the team, and re-enter the label and URL. It's worth keeping a note of important URLs somewhere outside the app. Tip: before an event opens, click each link once yourself to confirm it lands where you expect. Families lose trust fast in a "Schedule" link that 404s.

docs.text: Team Links Team Links let you post handy web links on your event's player-facing pages — things like a team's practice schedule, a video channel, a fundraising page, or a shared photo album. Each link can be attached to one team or shown to all teams , so families see exactly the links that apply to them. What a link holds Team — the team the link belongs to, or — All Teams — to show it everywhere. Label — the clickable text families see (keep it short and clear, e.g. "Practice Schedule"). URL — the full web address, starting with https:// . Adding and managing links Click Add , pick a team (or All Teams), enter a label and the URL, and save. Use Edit on any row to fix a label or a broken URL. Use Delete to remove a link that's no longer relevant — it disappears from the player pages. Paste the whole URL. Include https:// — a bare address like myteam.com/schedule may not open correctly for families. Common mistakes A partial URL. Without the https:// prefix the link can break. Copy the full address from your browser's address bar. Assigning to the wrong team. A link set to one team only shows on that team's pages — double-check the Team field, or use All Teams for event-wide links. Cryptic labels. "Click here" tells families nothing; name the destination so they know what they're opening.

docs.text: Team registration Adding a team to your Library is not the same as registering it. This trips up more club reps than anything else — the first two questions below are the fix. I added my team, but it's not in the event. What did I miss? Your Library is a reusable roster of teams — saving one there does not enter it in this event. A team is registered only when you give it an age group , using the blue Register button on the library team: Register How can I tell which teams are actually in the event? Watch which state each team is in: In your Club Library → click Register → Registered for this event Registered teams collect in the green Registered Teams card. If that card is empty, none of your teams are in the event — no matter how many sit in your library. The Library drawer footer still says "Close." Is that a problem? It's a signal. While the footer reads Close , you still have library teams that aren't registered. Once every team you intend to enter is registered, it changes to Done . Don't walk away on a Close if you meant to register more. What happens the moment I click Register? You pick a Level of Play and an Age Group , and the team is entered right then. That single action is the difference between "saved for later" and "playing." My team came back with a "WL" badge. Did something go wrong? No. The age group you chose is full, so instead of turning the team away, the system placed it on a WL waitlist. If a spot opens, the team can be moved off it. I registered a team into the wrong age group. How do I fix it? Age group is locked after registration, because it drives caps, waitlists, and fees. To correct it: remove the team from the event, then register it again with the right age group. The team stays in your library the whole time. Can I rename a team? Should my club name go in the name? You can rename a team in your library — but don't put your club's name in it . Schedules already show your club, so "Thunder" is right; "Riverside Thunder" reads as "Riverside Riverside Thunder" on the schedule. There's no Delete option — only Archive. Why? A team with event history can't be deleted, because that would erase the record. Instead you archive it, which retires it from view while keeping its history intact. Each team's menu explains why an action is unavailable. When and how do I pay? On the Payment step, which covers all your registered teams together. Depending on the event you can pay a deposit now to hold your spots, or the full balance . Teams still in your library aren't billed. Tip: before you close the browser, confirm every team you wanted is in the green Registered Teams card and the footer says Done . That one glance prevents the most common "my team never showed up" call.

docs.text: Registering your club's teams This wizard signs you in as a club representative and enters your teams into this event . Your event's name is shown in the banner at the top of every step so you always know which event you're registering for. The one thing to get right There are two separate actions, and it's easy to do the first and forget the second: In your Club Library A saved team record you can reuse every season. Not yet in this event. Registered for this event A library team you've given an age group for this event. This is what puts them on the field. Adding a team to your Library saves it for reuse — but it does not enter it in the event. A team is only registered once you give it an age group for this event. If your Registered Teams card is empty, none of your teams are in the event yet — no matter how many are in your library. The steps Club Rep Info — sign in (or create a club-rep account) and review your club. Waivers — if this event has a refund policy, read and accept it. (Skipped if it doesn't apply, or if you've already signed.) Teams — build your library and register teams into the event (see below). Payment — pay the deposit or full balance for your registered teams. Review — confirm, then Finish . On the Teams screen Your saved teams live in the Library drawer on the right. Each unregistered team has a blue Register button — use it to pick a Level of Play and Age Group for this event. That's the moment the team is entered. Registered teams appear in the green Registered Teams card. If the drawer's footer still says Close (not Done ), you have library teams that aren't registered yet — don't walk away until the ones you want are in the green card. A full age group places the team on a waitlist (shown with a WL badge) rather than turning it away. Common mistakes Adding to the library but not registering. The most common one — see above. Putting your club's name in the team name. Don't — schedules already show your club, so "Thunder" is right, not "Riverside Thunder." Changing an age group after registering. It's locked, because it drives caps, waitlists, and fees. To move a team, remove it and register it again. If you get stuck Each team's menu explains why an action is unavailable (for example, a team with event history must be archived rather than deleted). If something still isn't clear, the event's contact is listed on the event home page.

docs.text: 3rd Party Data Access Grants apply immediately — no confirmation step. Clicking Grant access or Re-Activate is the decision. If you click the wrong row, Inactivate it — that also takes effect immediately. Exactly what data does the third party get? Two things, per event: rosters — player and parent names and email addresses — but only for age groups you have flagged Third-Party Roster Access in the L-A-D-T Editor, and the event's full schedule . If no age groups are flagged, an active login still gets the schedule but no roster data. The third party I want isn't listed. How do I add them? You can't from this screen — it's reuse-only . It offers only logins that have already been authorized for your organization at least once. A first-time authorization is set up with your TSIC administrator; once it exists, it appears here and you manage it across events yourself. The same name shows on every row, even ones I haven't granted. Is that a mistake? No — that is deliberate. Your organization has one authorized third party, so the table names them on every row so you can see exactly who Grant access would authorize before you click. Whether access is actually live is shown by the chip beside the name: Active , Inactive , or Not granted . A name on its own grants nothing. What are the two lines under "3rd party login"? The first line is the person's name at the third party — the contact your organization agreed to release data to. The second, in a fixed-width font, is the login they sign in with, normally an email address. If an account has no name on file, the login moves up to the first line on its own. How do I switch an event from one provider to another? Inactivate the current provider on that event first, then grant the other. Each event allows only one active third party at a time — the console will refuse a grant while another login is still active on the event. Does Inactivate delete anything? No. It immediately stops the third party from signing in to that event, but the authorization history is kept — the row shows Inactive and a one-click Re-Activate . Data the third party already downloaded is not recalled by inactivating. What does "Access window ends" mean? The date the third-party login expires on that event. After it passes, the login can no longer sign in even if it is still marked Active. Only events with an open access window appear in this table. An active grant only ever releases some age groups' rosters. Why? Roster release is opt-in per age group: in the L-A-D-T Editor, each age group has a Third-Party Roster Access flag. Only flagged age groups are included in the download — a common setup releases graduating-year age groups to a recruiting service while keeping younger ones private. Who can use this screen? Organization-level administrators only. Per-event directors don't see it — granting an outside agency access to player data is an organization-level decision, and it covers every event the organization runs. Tip: when an event's recruiting period ends, come back and Inactivate the login rather than letting the access window run out — the "N active" badge at the top of the screen makes it easy to spot events still releasing data.

You manage it event by event : each row is one of your events with an open access window, and each event grants or withholds access on its own. You are releasing data about minors to an outside agency. Once downloaded, the data leaves your control. Review your organization's privacy policy before granting, and grant only to third parties your organization has actually agreed to work with. Schedule — the event's full schedule is included whenever access is active. Reading the table Active The listed login can sign in to this event and download now. The only action is Inactivate . Inactive This third party held access before but cannot sign in now. Re-Activate restores it in one click. Not granted No third party has access to this event yet. Who you are granting to Every row names the third party before you act — you never have to open a control to find out who is involved. The person's name is on the first line; their login, usually an email address, sits beneath it in a fixed-width font. If your organization has authorized one third party — the usual case — that name appears on every row and Grant access authorizes it. There is nothing to choose. If your organization has authorized more than one , the row lists them as radio buttons with every name visible at once. Choose one, then Grant access . Granting and removing access Grant access / Re-Activate take effect immediately — there is no extra confirmation step, so treat the click itself as the decision. Inactivate ends the third party's ability to sign in to that event immediately. The history is kept, so you can Re-Activate later without setting anything up again. Each event allows one active third party at a time . To switch providers, Inactivate the current one first, then grant the other. Access window ends is the date the login expires on that event regardless of its Active state. Rosters are released per age group — flag the intended age groups Third-Party Roster Access in the L-A-D-T Editor. Expecting a new provider to appear on its own. First-time logins aren't created here; contact your TSIC administrator to authorize a new third party. Reading a named row as an active grant. A row can name a third party and still be Not granted — the chip beside the name, not the name itself, tells you whether access is live. Forgetting to Inactivate after an event's recruiting period. Access continues until you Inactivate it or the access window ends — whichever comes first.

docs.text: Assign Timeslots No slot, nowhere to put the game. Timeslot capacity is what makes or breaks a build — and a play day with no slots at all produces no games and no error. Watch the warnings above the table. What exactly is a timeslot? One droppable game slot: a day, a field, and a start time. When the schedule builds, each game lands in an open slot. Create enough of them, across enough fields, to hold every game your event needs. Why can't I click Set Up Timeslots? This age group has no game dates yet. The days the setup dialog offers are derived from the dates in the card above — no dates, no days, nothing to configure. Add at least one date first, or clone dates in from another age group. How do I edit a single row in the timeslot table? You don't — the table is a read-out. Everything is set in the Edit Timeslots dialog: unticking a field on a day removes its slots, ticking it on another day creates them, and the start, interval and slots-per-field replace what used to be per-row editing. One way in means the table can never disagree with what's stored. Do I have to set timeslots up for each pool separately? No. Setup works at the age-group level and writes the slots to every pool in it. Pools only appear in the table's last column, so you can see which ones a given field/day row covers. Why do the three counts above the table disagree? They answer different questions. Game slots is how many games actually fit — the one to compare against your pairings. Field/day rows is what's on screen after folding. Pool timeslots is the raw stored count: fields × pools × days, which is what legacy displayed. Six pools sharing one field-hour is one game slot, not six. A row is highlighted and says pools are missing. What does that mean? That field, on that day, has timeslots for some of the age group's pools but not all of them. The pools without slots can't have games placed there. Open setup and save the day again to cover every pool. What do Every (interval) and Slots / field control? Every is the gap between game starts on a field — 60 minutes means 8:00, 9:00, 10:00. Slots / field is how many games that field runs on the day. Fields × slots is the day's total, and the dialog adds it up for you as you type. What is the Rnd column on a game date? The first round played on that date. Day 1 is Rnd 1; if three rounds run on Day 1 then Day 2 starts at Rnd 4. Each calendar date should have its own first round — the screen warns you when two dates share one, or when every date is still sitting on Round 1. What do the +D, +W and +R buttons on a date do? +D clones the date to the next day, +W to the same day next week, and +R clones it carrying the next round number. They're shortcuts for the two shapes most events have: a weekend, or a league that plays the same weekday for weeks. Does Clone to another age group add to what's already there? No — it replaces . If the target age group already has dates or timeslots, they're removed and these are put in their place; you'll get a confirmation naming how many are about to go. The upside is that cloning twice can't double anything up. A field isn't getting any games. Why? Most likely it has no timeslots on that day for this age group. A field must be both assigned to the event (in Manage Fields ) and ticked for that day in setup. Check the day's section in the table — if the field isn't listed, it isn't in play. It says there are timeslots on a day the age group doesn't play. Those rows are dead — the builder only reads slots for days that appear in the game dates, so it will never look at them. Either add the matching game date, or let the next setup save clear them. Tip: assign fields and settle pools first, then come here. The game-slot count only means something next to the games your pools and pairings actually need, and setup can only offer fields the event has been given.

docs.text: Assign Timeslots Step 3 of the Scheduling Checklist, and two jobs on one screen: which days an age group plays , and which field slots exist on those days for games to drop into. You work one age group at a time — pick it in the rail on the left; the badge next to each name is its pool count. Dates first, then slots. The days you can set up timeslots for are derived from the game dates above — not chosen separately. Add no dates and there is nothing to configure; add a Sunday date and Sunday appears in setup. The build engine reads timeslots the same way, so a row for a day you never play is never read at all. Age Group Game Dates The top card is the calendar for this age group. Add Date creates one; the row actions edit, delete, or clone it: +D — clone to the next day. +W — clone to the same day next week. +R — clone this date carrying the next round number. Rnd is the first round played on that date. Day 1 is Rnd 1; if three rounds run on Day 1, Day 2 starts at Rnd 4. Each calendar date should have its own first round — the screen warns you if two dates share one, or if every date is sitting on Round 1. Age Group Timeslots The bottom card is the inventory of droppable game slots. Set Up Timeslots (or Edit Timeslots once some exist) is the only way to create or change them — the table below it is a read-out, not an editor. The setup dialog lists one row per day this age group plays. For each day you set: Fields Which fields host this age group that day. Tick a field to add it; untick to remove it. Start The first game time on the day. Every Minutes between game starts on a field — the interval. Slots / field How many games each field runs that day. Fields × slots is the day's total, shown as you type. Saving writes the slots to every pool in the age group — you don't set them up pool by pool. The dialog totals the slots you're about to create so you can compare against the games your pairings need before you commit. A played day with no timeslots is a silent build failure. The builder places no games on it and says nothing. The screen calls it out above the table — "plays Sunday but has no timeslots there" — with a button straight into setup. The reverse case is flagged too: slots sitting on a day this age group has no game date for are dead rows the builder never reads. Reading the timeslot table Slots are stored per pool, so a 31-field age group with 6 pools is 186 near-identical rows. The table folds them: one row per field per day , with the pools it covers summarised in the last column. A row that doesn't cover every pool is highlighted and shows how many are missing. Three counts sit above the table and mean different things: Game slots — how many games actually fit. This is the number to compare against what your pairings need. Pools don't multiply it; six pools share the same physical field-hour. Field/day rows — what's on screen after folding. Pool timeslots — the raw stored rows. It's the number legacy displayed, and it's why the two don't match. Copying to another age group The Clone to control at the top copies this age group's Dates or its Fields to another age group. Set 2030 up the way you want it, then push it across. Cloning replaces the target — it never appends. If the target age group already has dates or timeslots, they're cleared and replaced with these. You get a confirmation naming what's about to be lost. Cloning the same thing twice is therefore safe; it can't double anything up. Common mistakes Setting up timeslots before dates. Setup is disabled until the age group has at least one game date, because the days it configures come from them. Too few slots for the games needed. Compare the game-slot count against what your pools and pairings require. A shortfall means the builder runs out of room. Leaving a play day empty. Heed the warning banner — a played day with no slots produces no games and no error. Assuming a clone merged. It replaced. If the target had dates you wanted to keep, they're gone — re-add them rather than cloning back and forth.

docs.text: Tournament Parking Analysis The numbers come from your schedule plus your assumptions. Change the buffers or cars-per-team and the projected peak changes with them. What do the Arrival and Departure buffers do? They set how long a team is counted as on-site around each game — Arrival Buffer minutes before it starts and Departure Buffer minutes after it ends. Longer buffers mean teams overlap more, which raises the projected peak. What's "Cars / Team"? The average number of vehicles a team brings. The tool multiplies on-site teams by this number to estimate cars, so set it to match your crowd — a youth event with parents carpooling looks very different from one where every player drives. Where do I see the busiest moment? Peak Cars On-Site and Peak Teams On-Site are the headline numbers — the worst-case load you need capacity for. The chart and grid show how load builds and clears across the day, per complex. The peak is higher than my lot holds. What can I do? A few levers: stagger start times in the Rescheduler to flatten the peak, arrange overflow parking, or staff the busy window. This screen tells you where and when the crunch is so you can plan for it in advance. It's showing nothing. Why? The analysis is built from scheduled games — if the schedule isn't built yet, there's nothing to project. Generate the schedule first, then come back. Tip: run this after scheduling but before you finalize start times. If a complex peaks over capacity, nudging a wave of games earlier or later in the Rescheduler is the cheapest fix — and this screen shows whether it worked.

docs.text: Tournament Parking Analysis This tool estimates how many vehicles and teams will be on-site at each field complex over your tournament days, so you can plan parking and staffing before crowds show up. It reads your built schedule and projects the load hour by hour. Listed under Tools on the Scheduling Checklist — it unlocks once the schedule has games, because there is nothing to project before that. The arrow beside the title takes you back. It's an estimate, driven by the schedule. The projection comes from your actual games plus a few assumptions you control — so it only means something once the schedule is built. The three assumptions you set Arrival Buffer — how many minutes before their game teams show up. Departure Buffer — how long they linger after it ends. Cars / Team — how many vehicles a team brings, on average. Together these decide how long each team "occupies" a complex around its games, and how that converts to cars. Tune them to match your event and the numbers update. What it shows Peak Cars On-Site and Peak Teams On-Site — the worst-case moment you need to plan for. A chart and grid of load over the day, per complex — switch tabs between All Complexes and each individual complex/day. How to use it Set realistic buffers and a cars-per-team figure for your crowd, then read the peak at each complex. If the peak outstrips a lot's capacity, you can stagger start times in the Rescheduler, add overflow parking, or staff the busy window. It's a planning lens, not a reservation system. Common mistakes Running it before the schedule exists. With no games, there's nothing to project — build the schedule first. Unrealistic assumptions. A too-low cars-per-team or too-short buffer understates the peak; set them to your actual crowd. Treating the estimate as exact. It's a well-reasoned projection to plan against, not a guaranteed count.

headings: Upload Uniform Numbers

My upload was rejected. What's wrong?
The results show some rows as Errors. What now?
What does "Unchanged" mean — did those players fail?
Is it safe to upload the same file twice?
docs.text: Upload Uniform Numbers Always start from a freshly downloaded template. The file has hidden columns the system needs to match each player. Type numbers into your own spreadsheet and the upload can't line rows up. Which columns do I fill in? Only UniformNo and DayGroup . Every other column — especially the ID column — must stay exactly as downloaded, since that's how each row is matched to the right player. My upload was rejected. What's wrong? Check three things: the file is a .xlsx (not .csv or .xls), it's under 10 MB , and its columns are unchanged from the template. Any of those will stop the whole file from being accepted. The results show some rows as Errors. What now? The Error Details table lists each bad row and the reason. Fix those rows in the spreadsheet and upload again — the rows that already applied stay applied, so re-uploading only catches up the ones that failed. What does "Unchanged" mean — did those players fail? No. "Unchanged" rows already had the number/group in the file, so there was nothing to update. It's a success, not an error — only the Errors count needs your attention. Is it safe to upload the same file twice? Yes. The upload just applies whatever's in the file; running it again sets the same values, so rows that already matched show as Unchanged. That's why fixing errors and re-uploading is the standard fix. Tip: if your roster changed since you last downloaded the template, grab a fresh one — a stale file won't contain players who registered after you downloaded it.

headings: Upload Uniform Numbers
How it works — two steps
Reading the results
Common mistakes
docs.text: Upload Uniform Numbers This tool sets uniform numbers (and day groups) for a whole event at once, using Excel instead of editing players one by one. You download a spreadsheet pre-filled with every registered player, type in their numbers, and upload it back — the system applies the changes in bulk. How it works — two steps Download Template — an Excel ( .xlsx ) file with a row for every player in this event. Fill in the UniformNo and DayGroup columns. Leave the other columns (including the ID column) exactly as they are. Upload File — drop the saved .xlsx back in (or click to browse) and choose Upload & Apply . Only .xlsx files up to 10 MB are accepted. Reading the results After an upload you get a summary: Updated — rows whose number/group changed. Unchanged — rows that already matched, so nothing to do. Errors — rows that couldn't be applied, listed below with the row number and a reason. Total Rows — everything the file contained. If there are errors, fix those rows in the spreadsheet and re-upload — re-uploading is safe and just re-applies. Don't touch the ID column. It's how the system knows which player each row belongs to. Change or delete it and those rows land in the Errors list. Common mistakes Uploading a different file format. It must be the .xlsx template — not a CSV, not an old .xls , not a re-saved copy that changed the columns. Editing or reordering columns. Only change UniformNo and DayGroup; leave the structure alone or the upload can't map rows. Starting from a stale template. Download a fresh template if your roster changed — an old file won't include newly-registered players.

docs.text: US Lax Membership Reconciliation This is the bulk tool. To check a single number without touching anyone's record, use the US Lax Membership Lookup instead. This page reconciles the whole roster and can email people. Who shows up in the candidate list? For Players, active lacrosse players with a membership ID on file. For Coaches, active unassigned adults with a USA Lacrosse number on file. Switching the role reloads the list for that group. What does Reconcile All actually change? It looks each membership up live at USA Lacrosse and updates the expiration date stored on the registrant. It doesn't change names, statuses, or anything else — those come from USA Lacrosse and are only displayed. The toast afterward tells you how many were checked and how many expiry dates changed. Why is someone flagged when their status is "Active"? Because their membership expires before this event's required date , or has no expiry on file. Active today isn't enough if it lapses before the event needs it — that's the same distinction the single-number lookup makes. I selected 40 rows but the summary says fewer were sent. Why? The server sends only to selected rows that both have an email and actually need action. Anyone already in good standing is skipped, and anyone without an email on file can't be reached. The send summary breaks down sent / failed / unsubscribed / no-email / skipped so you can see exactly what happened. Can I customize the email? Yes. The compose panel loads a default template (different for Players vs Coaches) with personalization tokens that fill in each recipient's details. Edit the subject and body freely — just keep the tone reporting status rather than accusing, since one message goes to people in several different situations. How do I keep a record of the results? Use the grid's Excel export to download the full reconciliation — every registrant, their status, involvement, and old/new expiry — for your files or to share with staff. Tip: reconcile, then click select rows needing action — it checks exactly the flagged people for you, so you email the right list without hand-picking rows.

docs.text: US Lax Membership Reconciliation This is the roster-wide version of the membership check. It looks up every registrant's USA Lacrosse membership in one pass, refreshes the expiration date on file, flags anyone whose membership isn't in good standing, and lets you email those people a ready-made message telling them how to fix it. The workflow Pick a role — Players or Coaches. Each loads its own eligible list (active registrants with a membership ID on file). Reconcile All — the tool pings USA Lacrosse for each candidate, updates expiry dates, and fills the grid with each person's status, age-verification, involvement, and old/new expiry. Review who needs action — rows are flagged when the check errored, the status isn't Active, there's no expiry on file, or the membership expires before this event's required date. Email them — use select rows needing action , open the compose panel (it pre-fills a role-appropriate template), and send. Each recipient gets a personalized message. People in good standing are never emailed — even if you select them. The server re-checks each recipient and skips anyone already Active and valid, so a broad selection won't spam families who are fine. Only those who genuinely need action receive a message. What "needs action" means A registrant is flagged when any of these is true: The USA Lacrosse lookup errored (couldn't be checked). Status is anything other than Active (Pending, Suspended, Inactive…). There's no expiration date on file. The membership expires before this event's valid-through date. Other actions Excel export the full reconciliation grid for your records or to share. The compose panel supports personalization tokens (name, membership ID, status, expiry) that fill in per recipient — the default template already uses them, and you can edit the wording. Common mistakes Emailing before reconciling. Run Reconcile All first so statuses and expiry dates are current — otherwise you're acting on stale data. Assuming selected = sent. Recipients without an email, or already in good standing, are skipped; the send summary tells you exactly who got a message. Editing the template into an accusation. The default copy deliberately reports status and lets each person self-route — keep that tone so it reads correctly for every recipient.

docs.text: US Lax Rankings Auto-matching is a suggestion, not a guarantee. It pairs by team name, and names are messy. Always review low-confidence and unmatched rows before you save, or you'll attach the wrong ranking to a team. What do high, medium, and low confidence mean? They reflect how closely a national ranking entry's name matched one of your teams. High lined up cleanly, medium is a likely match worth a glance, and low (or unmatched) needs you to confirm or fix it by hand. How do I match a team the tool missed? Click the team row to put it in match mode, then click the correct ranking in the sidebar. That pairs them as a manual match. If a team was matched to the wrong ranking, do the same to reassign it — the old ranking goes back to the sidebar. What's the difference between the save thresholds? High saves only high-confidence auto-matches (plus your manual ones). Medium adds the medium-confidence matches. All saves everything, including low-confidence guesses. Manual matches you made are always included regardless of threshold. I saved the wrong rankings — how do I start over? Use Clear rankings for the selected registered age group. It removes the saved ranking data from those teams so you can re-align and save fresh. What is the Season dropdown, and which one should I pick? The ranking site publishes one season at a time — "2025-26", "2024-25", and so on — and the Season list mirrors whatever they currently offer, defaulting to the newest. If you're seeding a new event, pick the most recently completed season: it has a full year of results behind it, where a season that has barely started has thin ratings. Switching season reloads the age group list, because the groups published differ from one season to the next. Why don't I see my event's age groups or the Find Matches button? Matching rankings to registered teams is available on tournament events only — it exists to seed pools. On any other event type you can still browse the published rankings; the matching controls are simply hidden. Can I just look at the rankings without matching anything? Yes. Choose a season and a ranking age group, and leave your event's age group unset — the published table appears on its own, with the same filter and sort. Nothing is written to your teams until you pick an age group and save. Nothing aligned — did it fail? Usually it means the two age groups don't correspond, or the national source has no entries for that group. Confirm you picked the right national list and the right registered age group, then re-align. Tip: save high-confidence first, then filter the table to unmatched and work that short list by hand. It's far faster than scanning every row, and you won't miss a team.

docs.text: US Lax Rankings This tool pulls published national club lacrosse rankings and attaches them to your registered teams, so you can build pools by team strength rather than by guesswork. It does the heavy lifting by auto-matching ranking entries to your teams; you review, fix the ones it wasn't sure about, and save. Saved rankings appear as Nat'l Rank in Pool Assignment. This is an experimental tool. The rankings are read live from a third-party website (usclublax.com) that we do not control. If they change their page layout, rename an age group, or go offline, results here can change or stop working without notice. Treat it as an aid to seeding, not a source of record — check the results before you rely on them, and use at your own discretion. Who can use it Browsing the published rankings works on any event — pick a season and an age group and the table appears. Matching those rankings to your registered teams is available on tournament events only, because seeding pools is what it exists for. On a non-tournament event the matching controls simply aren't shown. The workflow Pick a season. The ranking site publishes one season at a time, and the Season list mirrors what they currently offer — it defaults to the newest. When you're seeding a new event, choose the most recently completed season instead; it has a full year of results behind it. Note that the available age groups differ from season to season, so the age group list reloads when you switch. Pick two age groups. Choose the published ranking group, then the registered age group in your event it corresponds to. Published groups are named by graduation class — "Girls 2029" means the class of 2029 — so pair each with the age group holding those players. It auto-aligns as soon as both are chosen. Review the matches. Each of your teams shows the ranking it was paired with and a confidence — high, medium, or low — based on how closely the names matched. Fix the uncertain ones. For a team that didn't match (or matched wrong), click it, then pick the correct ranking from the sidebar. You can also undo a match to send it back. Save. Choose a threshold — high-confidence only, high + medium, or everything — and the rankings are written onto those teams. Manual matches you made are always saved too. Confidence tells you how much to trust an auto-match. Teams are paired by comparing club name, colour, graduation year and state. High = the names lined up cleanly. Medium = probably right, worth a glance. Low / unmatched = check it yourself before saving. Start by saving high-confidence, then work through the rest by hand. Other actions Browse without matching. Choose a season and a ranking age group and leave your event's age group unset — the published table appears on its own, with filter and sort, so you can look up where a club sits before you commit to anything. Filter the table to unmatched, high, or medium to focus your review. Export CSV to get the alignment as a spreadsheet. Clear rankings removes saved rankings from the selected age group's teams — a clean slate if an import went wrong. Common mistakes Saving everything blindly. "All" includes low-confidence guesses. Review low/unmatched first, or you'll pin the wrong ranking on a team. Mismatched age groups. Aligning a U15 national list against your U13 teams produces nonsense matches — pair like with like, and remember the published groups are by graduation class. Seeding off a season that has barely started. A season with few games played has thin ratings. Switch to the last completed season instead. Forgetting to save. Reviewing and matching on screen isn't persisted until you Save; leave without saving and the work is lost.

headings: US Lax Membership Lookup
What counts as a valid membership number?
The membership is "Active" but flagged as not valid — why?
What's the "valid-through" date it compares against?
I got "service temporarily unavailable." What now?

docs.text: US Lax Membership Lookup This checks one number at a time. It's a diagnostic lookup, not a bulk reconciler. For the whole roster, use the US Lax Membership tool. What counts as a valid membership number? A USA Lacrosse number of 6 to 12 digits. If you enter letters or the wrong length, the tool tells you before it even looks it up. The membership is "Active" but flagged as not valid — why? Because it expires before this event's valid-through date. Active means valid right now; the event needs it to stay active through a later date. A membership that lapses mid-season is active today but still won't cover the event. What's the "valid-through" date it compares against? It's a setting on the event — the date a membership must remain active past to satisfy this event's requirement. The page shows it so you know what the expiration is being measured against. If it reads "Not set," the event hasn't defined one. I got "service temporarily unavailable." What now? The lookup calls USA Lacrosse live, so a hiccup there stops the check. Wait a moment and try again — it's not a problem with the number you entered. Does looking a number up change the registrant's record? No. This page only reads and displays — it never writes anything back. Updating a registrant's membership status is done in the registrant's record or the US Lax Membership tool. Tip: keep this open when a parent calls about a membership dispute — you can read them the exact status and expiration on file with USA Lacrosse in seconds.

docs.text: US Lax Membership Lookup A quick spot-check for a single USA Lacrosse membership number. Type a number, verify it, and see whether it's active and whether it's valid long enough for this event . Use it when a family disputes a membership problem, or to sanity-check a number before you rely on it. How to use it Enter a USA Lacrosse membership number (6–12 digits) and click Verify (or press Enter). The result shows the member's status and expiration date straight from USA Lacrosse. It's compared against this event's valid-through date — the date a membership must remain active past. If the membership expires before then, it's flagged as not valid for the event. "Active" isn't the whole story. A membership can be active today but still expire before your event's valid-through date. This tool checks both, so you catch the ones that lapse mid-season. What it is (and isn't) This is a read-only lookup — it doesn't change a registrant's record or fix anything. To reconcile memberships across your whole roster or email people about missing ones, use the US Lax Membership tool instead. Common mistakes Mistyping the number. A single wrong digit returns the wrong person or no result — copy it exactly. Reading "Active" as "good for the event." Check the expiration against the event's valid-through date, which this page shows for you. Expecting it to update the registrant. It's a diagnostic; fixing the record happens elsewhere.
